title: Apple’s Black Friday Deal 2026: What to expect from its shopping event
content:
Macworld





The biggest shopping day of the year is Black Friday, which this year falls on Friday, November 27, 2026. If you are looking to buy an Apple product then Black Friday is a good time to buy. Apple typically runs a Black Friday-to-Cyber Monday shopping event.
The company usually offers gift cards with eligible purchases rather than lowering Apple Store prices. We don’t yet have details of Apple’s offer for 2026, but Apple’s 2025 promotion was announced on November 20, so this year we expect an announcement on or around Thursday, November 19. 
In 2025 Apple offered gift cards worth $25 to $250 in the U.S. (£20 to £200 in the U.K.), depending on the eligible product – including a $75 gift voucher with an iPhone 16, $100 with an iPad Air, and up to $250 with a MacBook Pro; third-party retailers, such as Amazon and Best Buy often provide direct discounts instead. Apple also offers education pricing, refurbished products, and trade-in credit.
For the latest discounts from other retailers, see our roundup of the best Black Friday Apple deals.


When will Apple announce its Black Friday 2026 offer? 
Apple’s 2025 promotion was announced on November 20, so this year we expect an announcement on or around Thursday, November 19.
The event is likely to run from November 27–30, if Apple follows its usual pattern. 
Once the deal is live you will be able to see details here:
 Get Apple's Black Friday offer (U.S.)
 Get Apple's Black Friday offer (U.K.)


							


Does Apple do a Black Friday sale?
Does Apple hold a Black Friday sale? We wish it would but, unfortunately, Apple’s Black Friday offer is usually a giveaway of Apple Gift Cards with certain purchases made during the Black Friday period. It gives away gift cards with select purchases from Black Friday to Cyber Monday each year, we expect it will do the same between November 27 and November 30 2026.
In 2025, the company gave away up to $250/£200 with Macs, $100/£80 with iPads and $75/£60 with iPhones. This was a better offer than in November 2024 when the company gave away gift cards with values up to $200/£160 with select purchases made in the Apple Store (online and in person) on Black Friday, as well as on the Saturday, Sunday and on Cyber Monday. You can see how much Apple gave away in 2025 compared to what it gave away in 2024, 2023 and 2022 below.
Apple often excludes recently launched products, although there are exceptions: Apple Watch Series 11 and AirPods Pro 3 qualified in 2025. That makes some of this fall’s launches less likely candidates for the 2026 promotion, but no eligible products or exclusions have been confirmed.


						

							


Is Apple’s Black Friday offer worth waiting for?
Apple usually gives gift cards with selected purchases rather than lowering prices, so waiting for Apple itself may not get you a cheaper price. Black Friday is often one of the strongest periods for Apple deals, though discounts can also appear through November, Prime Day and other sales. Consider an early offer if it is close to that model’s previous low; stock and popular configurations can run out, and the biggest reductions often apply to older or clearance models. 
In short: Compare retailer discounts with the value of Apple’s gift card before deciding. Treat the card as its full face value only if it covers spending you already planned, and compare the exact same model and configuration.


						

							


What was Apple’s Black Friday offer in 2025?

				
					

				
			Apple’s Black Friday offer.

Apple’s four-day Apple Store Shopping Event ran from Black Friday through Cyber Monday in 2025. Instead of cutting prices, Apple offered gift cards worth $25 to $250 (£20 to £200) with eligible purchases. You can see the qualifying products from 2025 in the table below. Ts&Cs are here.

Apple’s Black Friday deal 2025 vs 2024
Apple increased its maximum Black Friday gift card from $200/£160 in 2024 to $250/£200 in 2025. The highest value was available with MacBook Pro models featuring M4 Pro or M4 Max chips, so the increase didn’t benefit every purchase. It was a more generous incentive for eligible MacBook Pro buyers, although the gift card was credit toward future spending rather than a discount on the Mac itself.
The 2025 promotion also included some recent launches: Apple Watch Series 11, Apple Watch SE 3, and AirPods Pro 3 each came with a $50/£40 gift card, despite arriving just a few months earlier. Their inclusion shows that Apple doesn’t always exclude its newest products. That gives shoppers some reason to watch for offers on this year’s releases, although neither eligible products nor gift card values have been confirmed for 2026.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
When do the Black Friday sales begin? 
Black Friday officially begins on the day after Thanksgiving, which in 2026 is Friday, November 27. However, the sales begin well before that–we saw deals starting at the beginning of November. The main event runs through the weekend and concludes on Cyber Monday, which is November 30.





2.
Should I wait for Cyber Monday to purchase?
While it’s always possible that a better deal is waiting around the corner, if you see a good deal, don’t wait. While Cyber Monday promises impressive deals there’s always the risk that the Apple device you want sells out and you miss out on the great deal everyone else got.





3.
Are Apple’s Black Friday gift cards worth it?
Apple’s gift-card offers give you extra value on an eligible purchase rather than an immediate price cut.
A key benefit is flexibility: you can put the card toward another Apple product or services and digital purchases, such as subscriptions and App Store purchases.
That flexibility is most valuable if you expect to spend more with Apple. A gift card doesn’t lower the price you pay for the qualifying item, and it may be less appealing if you don’t plan to buy anything else from Apple; competing retailers may offer direct discounts instead.





4.
Can I use the gift card toward the product I’m buying?
No. The gift card can only be used for future purchases. 





5.
What can I buy with an Apple Gift Card?
An Apple Gift Card is remarkably versatile – it can be used to buy almost anything Apple sells, including hardware, services, subscriptions, and digital content.
This means you can use the balance toward:
Physical Apple products: iPhones, iPads, Macs, Apple Watches, AirPods, HomePods, Apple TV, and accessories like the Apple Pencil or Magic Keyboard .
Apple services and subscriptions: Apple Music, Apple TV+, iCloud storage, Apple Arcade, and Apple News+ .
Digital content: movies, music, games, apps, and in-app purchases from the App Store, iTunes Store, and Apple Books
The card can be redeemed to your Apple Account, and the balance never expires . It’s accepted at the Apple Store (online and in retail locations), the App Store, and across Apple’s digital storefronts.





6.
Where can I get the best Black Friday deals? 





Spotting a good Black Friday deal takes a bit of work but we’ll be doing most of it for you. title: How to stop your MacBook sleeping when the lid is closed
content:
Macworld





Many Mac users want to turn their MacBook into a desktop-style workstation, using an external display, keyboard, and mouse with the lid closed – a setup often called clamshell mode.
Running a MacBook this way can make sense for several reasons, from supporting multiple external monitors on certain Apple-silicon models to freeing up desk space and improving ergonomics. Others may want their Mac to keep working with the lid closed while it downloads files, runs backups, plays music, or so you can keep your AI agents running.
The problem is that macOS is designed to put a MacBook to sleep as soon as you close the lid. Apple does support clamshell mode (or closed-display mode), which lets you use a MacBook like a desktop by connecting an external display, keyboard, and mouse while the lid is closed. However, this setup comes with strict requirements: clamshell mode won’t work without an external monitor, and it can introduce performance or thermal trade-offs. If those limitations don’t suit your needs, there are alternative approaches – including third-party apps and system settings – that can keep a Mac awake with the lid closed. Just ensure that if your Mac is running in clamshell mode you do not put it inside a bag or enclosed space as it is likely to get hot. 
In this article we cover: What you need to use a MacBook with the lid closed, the steps to follow to use a MacBook with the lid closed, different methods to stop a Mac sleeping when the lid is closed, how to play music or continue a download while a MacBook lid is closed, and how to wake a MacBook with the lid closed.


Why would you want to use a MacBook with the lid closed?

				
					

				
			
Using a MacBook with the lid closed. 

Petter Ahrnstedt




There are several functional and technical reasons why you might choose to operate your MacBook with the lid closed.
Save desk space
Connecting an external display, keyboard and mouse lets you use your MacBook as a desktop computer. Closing the lid frees up space, particularly if you use a suitable vertical stand, while a larger monitor can provide a more comfortable working setup. Keep the Mac’s ventilation openings clear.
Keep tasks running
You may want downloads, backups, music playback or other tasks to continue while the lid is closed. A supported external-display setup keeps the Mac usable with the lid shut. Without an external display, you’ll generally need a utility that specifically supports closed-display operation, as explained below. Keep the Mac stationary and ventilated while it works; don’t put it in a bag.
Use multiple monitors
Multiple monitors give you more room to work and let you keep several apps visible without constantly switching between windows. You could write a document on one screen while consulting research on another, or keep email and chat separate from your main workspace. Closing your MacBook’s lid lets you work entirely on external monitors while freeing up desk space.
External display support depends on the chip. Base M4, M5 and M6 MacBook Pro models, plus M4 and M5 MacBook Air models, support two external displays. M5 Pro supports three; M1 Pro through M4 Pro support two; and M1 Max through M5 Max support four. Closing the lid doesn’t increase these limits.
Base M3 models support two external displays only with the lid closed, requiring Sonoma 14.3 or later on the Air and 14.6 or later on the Pro. Opening the lid disconnects the second monitor.
Base M1 and M2 MacBooks support one external display, although DisplayLink accessories and software offer a workaround. Resolution and refresh-rate limits vary; check individual specifications, particularly for Intel models.
See also: Best stands for MacBook and Best MacBook docking stations. 


						

							


Why does my MacBook sleep when I close the lid?
Apple doesn’t officially support disabling sleep when the lid is closed without an external monitor and power source by default, but there are workarounds. 
MacBooks are designed to enter a sleep state when the lid is closed primarily to manage power consumption and protect the hardware. This automatic transition helps preserve battery life and prevents the device from overheating while stored in a confined space like a backpack.
The reasons for this behavior include:
Power Management: Closing the lid triggers a standby mode that significantly reduces power usage.
Hardware Protection: If a MacBook remains active while closed in a bag, it can overheat and become really hot because it is still processing tasks without adequate ventilation.
Automatic Updates: While asleep, macOS may occasionally wake the system to install updates or sync data, though this can sometimes lead to the device becoming unexpectedly warm if it doesn’t return to sleep properly.


						

							


What do I need to use a MacBook with the lid closed: Clamshell Mode

				
					

				
			You’ll need an external monitor (or two), a mouse and keyboard to use a MacBook with the lid closed. 
Foundry




To operate your MacBook with the lid closed, you must have specific external hardware connected and meet the following requirements:
Power Source: Apple’s recommended setup for using a MacBook in closed-display (clamshell) mode is to connect an external display, a power adapter, and an external keyboard and mouse or trackpad. While some newer MacBook models — particularly Apple Silicon systems — may continue to operate with the lid closed while running on battery power, this behaviour can vary depending on the Mac model, macOS version, and connected peripherals. For the most reliable and fully supported clamshell-mode experience, Apple recommends keeping the MacBook connected to power.
External Display: The Mac must be connected to an external monitor.
External Peripherals: You must have an external keyboard and mouse (wired or Bluetooth) to wake and control the computer.
Up-to-date software: Using a MacBook with the lid closed is a lot simpler than it used to be if you are using a newer Mac and a newer version of the Mac operating system. In fact, if you are experiencing issues using your Mac with the lid closed then it is likely that you could address this by updating your Mac to a recent version of macOS, assuming your Mac supports it (see our macOS compatibility checker).  Newer versions of macOS have made this process much smoother, resolving many of the bugs that plagued older Intel-based MacBooks.


						

							


How to use a MacBook with the lid closed
Follow these steps to use your laptop as a desktop computer by connecting it to external peripherals while the built-in display is shut.
Connect your MacBook to power. Use its charger, or a compatible USB-C monitor or dock that supplies power to the Mac.
With the lid open, connect your external display, keyboard and mouse or trackpad. If you use Bluetooth peripherals, make sure they are paired with your Mac.
Turn on and unlock your MacBook. On Apple silicon models, click Allow if macOS asks permission for a connected accessory to connect.
Wait until your Mac’s desktop appears on the external display, then close the lid.
The external display may briefly go dark. If your desktop doesn’t reappear, press a key on the external keyboard or click the mouse to wake the Mac.
You can read more about using a second display with your Mac here.
But even with these settings, if you aren’t attached to an external monitor closing the lid will cause the Mac to sleep.
What if you don’t want to plug in an external display? Read on… 


						

							


How to stop a MacBook from sleeping when the lid is closed 
Suppose you don’t want your MacBook to sleep when you close the lid? Maybe it is busy downloading something and you don’t want it to stop. Or maybe you’ve left it downloading an update overnight or syncing your Time Machine backup, and you’d prefer not to see the backlit keyboard. In another scenario you might want to play music from the MacBook without having to have the lid open – something likely to appeal to a few DJs.
The problem is that your Mac will go to sleep when you close the lid if it’s not plugged in and connected to an external display.
To stop a MacBook from sleeping when the lid is closed – specifically when it is running on battery power and not connected to an external monitor – you generally need to use third-party software or advanced system commands. By default, macOS is designed to enter sleep mode in this state to preserve battery life and prevent overheating.


						

							


Option 1: Use a Third-Party App like Amphetamine
A utility that supports closed-display operation can keep your MacBook awake with its lid closed. Our recommendation is Amphetamine, which is free and can be downloaded from the Mac App Store:
As noted in our round up of the best free Mac apps, Amphetamine will keep your Mac awake. Featuring a menu bar-based interface, the app lets you temporarily override your Mac’s sleep schedule (even when your MacBook’s lid is closed) and even adds a few useful features like activating only when connected to specific Wi-Fi networks and keeping only certain drives awake.
Free at  Mac App Store						
					
To configure Amphetamine for this specific scenario, follow these steps:
Download and open Amphetamine (it’s on the Mac App Store).
Click the pill-shaped icon in your menu bar
Select Quick Settings.
In the Session Defaults section, uncheck the box for “Allow system sleep when display is closed”.
Start a new session using “Indefinitely” or “While File is Downloading” or “While App is Running”) to keep the Mac awake after closing the lid.
Your Mac may need to be plugged in while the download continues. 
On Apple silicon MacBooks, connecting or disconnecting external power can affect Amphetamine’s closed-display sessions. The developer offers an optional Power Protect helper to address this behavior. Follow the guidance presented by the app, and check that your session continues after closing the lid or changing power sources.
Alternatively, Caffeinated is a paid app available on the Mac App Store here for $3.99/£4.49. Version 3.2 introduced an option to keep your MacBook awake with the lid closed. Enable its closed-lid option for this purpose.


						

							


Option 2: Use a dongle
You can use a dummy display plug that tricks your MacBook into thinking it’s connected to an external display, thus putting your MacBook in clamshell mode and keeping it running.
You can find a four-pack of UGreen HDMI dummy adapters on Amazon for nine bucks.


						

							


Option 3: Use Terminal Commands
If you prefer not to install third-party software, you can use the Terminal to disable sleep mode entirely.
Open Terminal. 
Enter the following command: sudo pmset -a disablesleep 1
That should stop your Mac sleeping. 
Please note that using this command will prevent the Mac from sleeping in all scenarios until you reverse it by entering: 
sudo pmset -a disablesleep 0


						

							


Can Battery settings keep a MacBook awake with the lid closed?
In System Settings > Battery > Options, “Prevent automatic sleeping on power adapter when the display is off” keeps your plugged-in Mac awake when its screen turns off. 
However, this setting alone does not override sleep triggered by closing the lid. 
For closed-lid use, follow the external-display setup above or use a utility that specifically supports closed-display operation.


						

							


How to play music with your Mac’s lid closed
You can use the free Amphetamine app (mentioned above) to keep your Mac awake while the display is closed, here’s how:
Once installed on a Mac you will find a pill-shaped icon in the menu bar at the top of the screen. You can choose from options such as Start New Session While File is Downloading or While App is Running.
If you want to keep Music (or what app you are using) running with the lid closed, first, you need to have that app open. Then follow these steps:
Click on the Amphetamine icon in the menu bar.
Click on Quick Settings.
In the Session Defaults section, deselect “Allow system sleep when display is closed.”
Go back to the main menu and select While App is Running and pick Music or the app you are using. If your app is not open, it will not appear in the list. Only apps that are running appear.
You will now be able to shut your Mac’s lid and continue listening to Music. 

				
					

				
			
Foundry



							


How to continue a download with a MacBook lid closed

				
					

				
			
Foundry




By default, macOS puts your MacBook to sleep when you close the lid. In sleep mode, most apps stop running, which means regular downloads in Safari, Chrome, Steam, or other apps will usually pause.
To keep downloads running with the lid closed, you need to prevent your Mac from fully sleeping.
Your best option is to use a third-party app, like Amphetamine. Follow the steps in the section above and start a session by selecting While File is Downloading or While App is Running (select your browser or download manager).
“Wake for network access,” found in System Settings > Battery > Options, allows your Mac to wake briefly so other users can access shared services. It does not keep the Mac continuously awake or override sleep when you close the lid. Don’t rely on it to keep browser or game downloads running; those require the Mac to remain awake.
With a utility such as Amphetamine preventing sleep the following downloads can continue: 
browser downloads
cloud storage syncs
Steam/game downloads
large file transfers and uploads


						

							


How to wake a MacBook with the lid closed

				
					

				
			You can use a Mac while it’s closed.

Halyna Kubiv




If your MacBook is asleep, you can usually wake it without opening the lid when it is connected to an external display, power, and an external keyboard and mouse or trackpad.
Make sure the external display is switched on and the MacBook is receiving power.
Press a key on the external keyboard or click the mouse or trackpad.
If the Mac doesn’t wake, open the lid and check its power, display and accessory connections.
These steps wake a sleeping MacBook. If it has been shut down, open the lid and press the power button if it doesn’t start automatically.
For scheduled startup and wake-up, see our separate guide to scheduling your Mac to turn on and off. If FileVault is enabled, you must log in after startup.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
Can a MacBook run with the lid closed without an external monitor?
By default, a MacBook is designed to enter sleep mode as soon as the lid is closed to preserve battery life and prevent overheating. Apple does support a closed-display mode (aka clamshell mode), but with hardware requirements that typically include an external monitor. However, there is third-party software, such as Amphetamine, that will allow you to override the default sleep schedule, keeping the system active even when the lid is shut and no external display is present.  





2.
Is it safe to stop a MacBook sleeping with the lid closed?
Yes. Apple supports using a MacBook with its lid closed when connected to an external display and accessories. Keep it on a hard, flat surface with ventilation openings unobstructed, and never leave it running inside a bag.
Thermal performance depends on the model and workload, though. Geekerwan, as reported by Macworld, found a closed-lid cooling advantage for the PROLED XDR MacBook Pro over the older mini-LED model tested.





3.
Why does my external monitor turn off when I close my MacBook?
If the external display goes dark when you close the lid, check that your MacBook is receiving power, the display is connected correctly, and an external keyboard and mouse or trackpad are available. A compatible USB-C display or dock may supply power without a separate charger. 
On Apple silicon models, open the lid and unlock the Mac to approve connected accessories if prompted. Then close the lid and try waking it with the external keyboard or mouse.





4.
Can I use clamshell mode on battery power instead of plugging in the charger?
In some cases, yes. Certain newer MacBook models – particularly Apple Silicon models – may continue to operate in clamshell mode while running on battery power. However, Apple’s recommended and officially supported setup for closed-display includes connecting the MacBook to a power adapter. 
Behaviour on battery power can vary depending on the Mac model, macOS version, and connected peripherals, so using external power is the most reliable configuration for clamshell mode.





5.
What’s the difference between sleep mode, clamshell mode, and preventing sleep on a MacBook?
The primary difference between these modes lies in how the MacBook manages its power, display, and background tasks when the lid is closed.
Sleep Mode: Sleep mode is the default state for a MacBook when the lid is closed. In this state, the system pauses most operations to conserve battery life.
Clamshell Mode: This mode allows you to use your MacBook as a desktop workstation while the lid is closed. This mode is officially supported by Apple but requires specific external hardware to function, including an external display, a power source, and external peripherals like a keyboard and mouse. 
Preventing Sleep: In some cases you might want to keep a MacBook fully active even when the lid is closed, without necessarily meeting the strict hardware requirements of clamshell mode. Since macOS doesn’t support this you need a third-party app, or you could plug in a dongle that makes your Mac think you have a display plugged in.

title: HomeView is Apple’s first post-iPhone device
content:
Macworld





On November 13, Apple will finally start shipping its long-awaited HomeView smart home hub. While the leaks gave us an early look at some of its specs, the official launch exposed its underlying philosophy through distinct hardware and software choices. Although the HomeView is unmistakably designed for iPhone users, its unique direction ushers in an all-new product type built for a future when Apple’s iconic handset doesn’t exist.
New yet familiar
The iPhone is by far Apple’s most influential product, and it will likely remain so for a very long time. Because of that legacy, every major Apple device released since its debut has felt like an iteration of the iPhone in one way or another—tweaked to accommodate a specific purpose. For example, many users continue to perceive the iPad as a large-canvas iPhone, while the Apple Watch essentially doubles as a mini iPhone strapped to your wrist. The Vision Pro similarly follows this direction, sharing familiar UIs, the App Store, and common Apple feature sets, acting as an advanced spatial iDevice of sorts. Even the MacBook now has a Dynamic Island.
We’ve reached a point where most of us are surrounded by screens all day long. Whether we’re working during daylight hours or winding down in the evening, chances are we’re facing some kind of rectangular display. Many of us now live in digital bubbles, privately consuming online content and increasingly detaching from our real-life surroundings. Apple’s HomeView doesn’t contribute to the rampant isolation; it discourages it and breaks the longstanding cycle.

				
					

				
			
Apple’s HomeView ad was an exaggerated view of a family’s frenetic morning routine—but no one was using an iPhone.

Apple




If you’ve seen Apple’s frenetic ad, you noticed that the featured family was using the HomeView in tandem. The home hub harmoniously switched between different user profiles and executed all kinds of tasks in an open, social manner. They could all tell what each member was generally up to based on their voice commands, but private details like iMessages remained solely visible to the active user.
Unlike the Apple TV 4K, the HomeView isn’t designed for long usage sessions. While it supports video streaming, it’s the first Apple product to offer an awkward 7-inch square screen, making it impractical for media consumption and other immersive experiences. It’s meant to keep you present in the moment with other household members around you.
Early preview
The HomeView expectedly borrows app icons and other features from the iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch, but it doesn’t behave like any traditional Apple device.
The original iPhone did not offer an App Store and instead limited its users to the core apps included at launch. Likewise, it took the Apple Watch years to support untethered apps and provide a dedicated App Store on watchOS. That, however, does not mean that the HomeView will ultimately follow suit and introduce an App Store. After all, the smart home hub has reportedly been ready for around two years and was only held back due to Siri AI’s delayed release. Apple had plenty of time to port its digital storefront’s foundation to the new platform, but it made a conscious decision to maintain the virtual shackles.
Opening the floodgates would bridge the gap between the HomeView and iPad, which would defeat its whole purpose. Apple doesn’t want the HomeView to become your next TikTok doom-scroll destination. And barring third-party smart home management apps that encourage users to invest in its HomeKit ecosystem—reinforcing its walled garden further.

				
					

				
			
HomeView bridges the screen in your pocket and the people in your house.

Foundry




A Siri-centric future
HomeView’s support for CarPlay extensions and App Intents in compatible iPhone apps via Siri AI suggests that the App Store’s omission is a deliberate move to also push third-party developers to fully adopt App Intents in their software. Otherwise, users likely won’t be able to easily interact with their apps using the smart home hub.
As more developers build for Siri AI and its reliability improves, users will have fewer reasons to pick up their iPhones. They’ll be able to conveniently communicate with others, adjust plans, and make reservations by simply talking to the tiny display in the center of the room. Apple could also potentially minimize the reliance on nearby iPhones by indexing data stored in iCloud, which includes messages, emails, events, reminders, notes, photos, files, and much more. Gemini can already tap into Google Workspace data from any device, and Apple could realistically build a similar infrastructure down the road.
By the time Apple’s rumored smart glasses and other AI gadgets debut, presumably enough developers will have embraced App Intents and Siri AI, all thanks to the HomeView. This will make these fresh concepts—which will primarily operate with Siri’s assistance—fully functional and practical from day one, increasing their popularity and appeal among consumers. Despite beating with an iPhone’s A18 heart, the HomeView is secretly architecting a world where the iPhone stays in our pocket—or perhaps doesn’t exist at all.

title: Apple Support Community Deserved a Proper Goodbye
content:
Apple on Tuesday abruptly placed the Apple Support Community into a read-only state and announced that the forums will be permanently closing on Friday, November 20. Those who contributed to the site — some for more than two decades — were blindsided by this decision and had no chance to post farewell messages.


Even if you felt the Apple Support Community contained too many generic or unhelpful answers from users trying to boost their post counts and earn points, the people volunteering their time to the site still deserved a proper goodbye.

Below, we have highlighted some of those people and their experiences.

Jeff Donald from Florida was a member of the Apple Support Community since November 2000, when the forums were still known as Apple Discussions. This past year, Apple recognized his efforts by inviting him to the Apple Community+ program, which launched in 2022 and provided members with a few extra perks and experiences.

Leroy Douglas was a member since July 2009. He said he was a bit shocked to see Apple's sudden announcement, but he saw the writing on the wall.

Tobias Steen in Germany said there were also Apple Support Communities in Chinese, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. For some reason, the French and German versions do not have closure notices, but we are told they will meet the same fate.

Evan Bato Rousseau in France to 83-year-old Nobel Prize winner Sir Tim Hunt in England, who told us he found it to be a helpful resource, even if some of the answers were wonky.

John Daniel, the Canadian developer of macOS diagnostic tool EtreCheck, said he was active in the Apple Support Community for more than two decades. Users like him who reached "Level 6" or higher based on their contributions received access to The Lounge, a private category of forums where Apple employees sometimes participated.

Prior to 2020, John said Apple occasionally hosted in-person meetups for Support Community members, including a special visit to Apple Park. 

"I don't agree with comments that so many are making about the Apple Support Community right now," he said, in response to those who described it as useless. "We regularly solved problems, identified significant issues with Apple projects, traced the cause of bugs and fixed them, and always learned new things. That's what I'm going to miss."

Elías Rojano Núñez of Chile participated in the Spanish forums. He told us that he found it deeply satisfying when he was able to help others, and he was saddened that the Spanish forums were shuttered without any advanced notice, but he is grateful for the opportunity that he had and will always value the interactions he had with fellow contributors.

Rojano Núñez shared a photo of some of the items he received from Apple over the years, including a 5-year Apple Support Community anniversary pin. There were also 10-year, 15-year, and 20-year pins. Over the years, merchandise given out included Apple-branded hats, shirts, tote bags, and even umbrellas once.


Whatever its shortcomings, the Apple Support Community was more than just a place to ask questions. For some, it was a place to belong.

good riddance.
This article, "Apple Support Community Deserved a Proper Goodbye" first appeared on MacRumors.com

title: Best time to buy an iPhone in 2026: Buy now or wait for Black Friday?
content:
Macworld





If you’re planning to buy a new iPhone, should you buy now or wait for Black Friday? The iPhone Duo went on sale on October 23, completing Apple’s latest launches, but availability and early reports of inner-display failures complicate the decision for foldable buyers.
The Duo joins the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, although limited launch stock means getting Apple’s first foldable could require patience. Meanwhile, there are some excellent U.K. deals on the discontinued iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max as retailers clear remaining stock. If you want premium cameras and performance without paying the latest Pro prices, those older models are worth considering.
Apple rarely discounts its newest iPhones directly, and its 2026 price increases have made choosing carefully even more important. Black Friday may bring better offers, particularly through carriers and trade-in promotions, but a strong discount on the right phone can make buying now worthwhile.
In this guide, we explain whether now is a good time to buy each iPhone, which models are worth waiting for, and when to expect the best deals. We’ll help you weigh the appeal of Apple’s newest hardware against the savings available on older models.
When to buy an iPhone in 2026-2027: At a glance

 Best times to buy the iPhones in 2026 and 2027.






The worst time to buy an iPhone
This is generally in the weeks leading up to Apple’s September launch event, or in the early spring, when new models are expected to be announced. Buying just before a refresh means you could miss out on new features or pay full price for a model that’s about to be superseded.
The best time to buy an iPhone 
This depends on where you live:
In the U.K., where most iPhones are sold unlocked and off contract, the biggest savings are typically available during major sales events such as Amazon Prime Day (usually in July and October, and occasionally in March) and Black Friday in late November. However, worthwhile iPhone discounts can be found throughout the year if you know where to look.
In the U.S., where people tend to buy iPhones through a carrier, the best time to upgrade is often during Black Friday when networks enhance their offers with larger trade-in values, bill credits, gift cards, or discounted service plans. 
Due to the Black Friday sales, November and December could be a particularly good time to grab a deal on an older iPhone, such as the iPhone 17 Pro or iPhone 17 Pro Max. 


						

							







Should you buy a new iPhone now or wait? 
Wait for Black Friday, November 27, 2026.  

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




September and the months that follow are a much better time to buy an iPhone than earlier in the summer (July and August are usually poor months to buy a Pro iPhone because Apple’s September launch is so close). The iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo have now been unveiled, removing that uncertainty.
If you need a phone now, there’s little reason to wait for another annual refresh, and the iPhone 17, 17e and Air are also relatively safe purchases because their successors aren’t expected until spring 2027. See: iPhone 18 and 18e rumors and iPhone Air 2 rumors. 
The iPhone 17 remains the strongest value, with a 120Hz ProMotion display, A19 chip, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage for $899/£899 (although it was previously $799/£799). The 18 Pro and Pro Max make more sense if you want the best cameras, performance or battery life, while the Duo is for buyers specifically interested in Apple’s new folding design.
There is, however, one important reason to wait: 2027 could bring a much bigger iPhone redesign. Apple is rumored to be preparing a 20th-anniversary iPhone – the iPhone 19 or 20 with a near-all-screen curved design, under-display Face ID, possible solid-state buttons, a thinner and more efficient OLED display, a larger battery and major camera improvements. That could make 2027 a more significant upgrade year than 2026.
So if your current iPhone is still serving you well, waiting could be worthwhile. If you need a phone now, wait until Black Friday if price is your main concern.

Should you wait for the iPhone 18?
For most people, there isn’t a strong reason to wait for the iPhone 18. Apple isn’t expected to launch the standard model until spring 2027, so buying an iPhone 17 before the end of 2026 would still give you several months with Apple’s current mainstream model before its replacement arrives.
The iPhone 18 is expected to bring a 2nm A20 chip, potentially 9GB or 12GB of RAM, Apple’s C2 modem and possibly a new 24MP front camera. Extra RAM could prove particularly useful for future Apple Intelligence and Siri features. However, the rear camera system is still expected to consist of two 48MP cameras, while the display may remain broadly similar to the iPhone 17’s 6.3-inch ProMotion panel.
There is also some uncertainty over exactly what the iPhone 18 lineup will look like. A September 2026 rumour suggested Apple could effectively merge the standard iPhone and iPhone Air into a single model, rather than continuing them as two separate devices. If that happens, the iPhone 18 could adopt some of the Air’s thinner, lighter design while retaining the broader appeal of the standard iPhone. For now, though, that remains speculative.
Price is another consideration. With the arrival of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, Apple increased iPhone prices across the range, so the iPhone 17 now costs $899, $100 more than at launch. When the iPhone 18 arrives, it is likely to inherit that $899 price point, while the iPhone 17 could drop back to around $799 at which you may regret buying it at the higher price.
Wait if you want the newer A20 chip, potentially more RAM, an improved front camera, or are intrigued by the possibility of a thinner redesigned standard model. 
Don’t wait if you simply want ProMotion, dual 48MP cameras, excellent battery life and 256GB of storage as standard – the iPhone 17 already delivers all of that.

 FAQ 


1.
When is the best carrier upgrade timing? 
Apple typically announces new iPhone models in September. Carriers often roll out their most aggressive trade-in offers and promotional deals around this time to entice customers to upgrade.
New releases: Waiting for the September (or spring) launch window is generally a good strategy if you want the latest model at a potentially better subsidized price.
Check your contract cycle: Many carrier contracts today last 24 to 36 months. If you’re nearing the end of your contract, you’re in a strong position to negotiate or take advantage of upgrade offers. However, upgrading mid-contract may involve paying off the remaining balance, so it’s worth checking your specific terms.
Consider Apple’s upgrade plans: Apple has replaced its old iPhone Upgrade Program with newer financing and leasing options. In the U.S., Apple Upgrade lets you lease an iPhone through Klarna and upgrade, buy or return it at the end of the term. In the U.K., Apple’s Flexible Finance Account offers eligible iPhones on monthly payment plans with the option to upgrade after a set number of payments. Terms and monthly costs vary by model.





2.
When does Apple update the iPhone?
Apple typically unveils new iPhones at a dedicated Apple event in September. Preorders usually open the following Friday, with devices shipping and arriving in stores a week later. However, some models arrive later: Apple announced the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and iPhone Duo in September 2026, but the Pro models went on sale September 18, while the Duo followed on October 23.
Apple also launches iPhones earlier in the year, particularly its more affordable models. The iPhone 16e arrived in February 2025 and the iPhone 17e in March 2026. The standard iPhone 18, iPhone 18e and iPhone Air 2 are expected in spring 2027.
These spring launches are often announced via press release, although Apple has also held spring events. Availability typically follows within one to two weeks, but initial supplies can be limited.
Compatible iPhones also receive a major iOS update each year, usually in September, bringing new features that can give an older phone a fresh lease of life.
Read our guide to the next Apple event to find out what’s coming next.





3.
When do iPhone prices drop and by how much?
Based on past experience, Apple is very unlikely to reduce the price of a new iPhone during its first year on sale.
However, when Apple introduces a new generation of iPhones, it usually cuts the price of the previous year’s models. That means September has traditionally been the point when older iPhones become cheaper.
Apple also tends to keep launch prices broadly similar from one generation to the next, at least in the U.S., although exchange rates and other regional factors can affect pricing elsewhere.
In 2024, for example, Apple reduced the price of the iPhone 15 and iPhone 15 Plus by $100/£100 when the iPhone 16 and 16 Plus arrived. The iPhone 16 also fell in price following the launch of the iPhone 17 in 2025. However, because the iPhone 17 doubled the base storage to 256GB, the older iPhone 16 looked less attractive even at $100/£100 less.
In 2026, the pattern changed. Apple actually raised iPhone prices, blaming higher memory costs. Even the year-old iPhone 17 and two-year-old iPhone 16 increased by $100, showing that older iPhones don’t always become cheaper when a new generation arrives.





4.
Is it better to buy from Apple or a carrier?
In the U.S., buying from Apple is usually the better option if you value flexibility. If you pay in full or use Apple’s own financing, the iPhone is unlocked, so you can switch carriers or use another eSIM when traveling. Apple also accepts trade-ins and, importantly, many AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon promotions are available when buying through Apple.
However, an iPhone bought from Apple but financed through an AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon device-payment plan is locked to that carrier until it has been paid off. An iPhone bought outright from Apple isn’t.
The main reason to buy directly from AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon is to take advantage of a particularly good promotion. U.S. carriers frequently advertise large trade-in credits or “free” iPhones, especially when you add a line or switch networks. The catch is that the discount is usually provided as monthly bill credits over 24 or 36 months, so if you leave early you can lose the remaining credits.
In the U.K., Apple sells iPhones unlocked and SIM-free, allowing you to shop separately for a SIM-only plan from EE, Vodafone, O2, Three or an MVNO. This makes it easier to switch networks and can work out cheaper over the life of the phone than bundling the handset and airtime into a single contract.
Apple isn’t necessarily the cheapest place to buy, however. Amazon U.K. and other retailers frequently discount SIM-free iPhones, and there can be substantial savings during sales events such as Black Friday.
Networks can also offer compelling promotions, including enhanced trade-in values, discounted airtime, generous data allowances or lower monthly payments. But make sure you compare the total cost of the contract, rather than focusing on the headline monthly price.





5.
When are the best iPhone deals?
The earliest you could expect to get a discount on the newest iPhones is around Black Friday at the end of November, so you might be planning to hold out until then. However, the deals we tend to see, if any, are usually for older handsets. See our round-up of Best Black Friday iPhone deals for more.
Nor should you expect to get a discount in an Apple Black Friday sale. Apple’s Black Friday sale usually only takes the form of vouchers with select product purchases, rather than a discount, and it is unlikely that the newest iPhone would qualify as in previous year’s new iPhones haven’t been included. 
Note that while shopping events like Black Friday get all the attention, that’s not the only time you can get discounts on Apple products: we see discounts all the time. Another event where we see good iPhone deals is Prime Day, which happens in June or July and October every year. So take a look at the iPhone deals for Amazon Prime Day sale to see what you might be able to save.
In our experience, we don’t tend to see discounts on the newest handset until the spring – and these are always from third-party resellers, never from Apple. In fact, we don’t tend to see the iPhone discounted in the U.S. very often, most of the discounts we see are in the U.K. where unlocked iPhones are often sold off-contract at a good discount.





6.
Is it worth buying a refurbished iPhone? 
Yes, buying a refurbished iPhone is absolutely worth it for most people, especially if you want to save money without sacrificing quality. 
Buying refurbished is a great way to “pick up a bargain” while still getting a premium device. You can typically save 15% to 30% compared to buying new, and sometimes much more on older models. 
A common misconception is that refurbished is the same as buying a used phone from a stranger, though. It’s not. A used phone is sold “as-is,” with no guarantee it will work properly. A refurbished phone has been professionally inspected, tested, and repaired if needed, and it comes with a warranty. 
If you want the highest quality, Apple’s own refurbished store is the gold standard.





7.
How to check iPhone stock near you
If the iPhone you want has a long delivery estimate, independent stock-checking services can help you find availability elsewhere. Apple Inventory Check lets you search Apple Store stock by country, location, model, color and storage capacity. It covers Apple’s current iPhone range, including the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and older models.
Checking nearby stores or choosing a different color or capacity could help you get your phone sooner. Confirm availability through Apple before traveling. For more options, see our guide to iPhone stock-checking services.





Conclusion: When is the best time to buy a new iPhone?
The worst time to buy is usually between July or August, mainly because with new iPhones on the horizon the price of the older handsets are likely to drop very soon.
If you want the newest iPhones then the best deals don’t tend to come before the spring and summer months. If you are happy to buy an older iPhone then you will probably see decent deals around Prime Day and Black Friday – but deals happen all year round. 
We hope this article has proved helpful in reaching an informed buying decision. Remember that good prices can be found all year round, if a retailer is feeling generous and you know where to look: read our guide to the best iPhone deals for more on that.

title: Apple employee charged with murder following fatal accident near Apple Park
content:
After an accident near the Apple Park Visitor Center, which resulted in the death of a toddler, an Apple employee was arrested and subsequently charged with murder.


An accident occurred near the Apple Park Visitor Center on Friday.
On Friday, Apple employee Eric Chen Su reportedly drove at around 100 miles per hour as he crashed into a vehicle stopped in front of him. While Su sustained light injuries, the occupants of the vehicle he struck, a two-year-old and her babysitter, were rushed to a nearby hospital.

title: Apple on Fatal Vehicle Crash Near Apple Park: 'Our Hearts Are Broken'
content:
Apple employee Eric Chen Su was arrested and charged with suspicion of gross vehicular manslaughter last week following a fatal collision near the intersection of North Tantau Avenue and Pruneridge Avenue, right next to the Apple Park Visitor Center, according to the Santa Clara County Sheriff's Office and the San Francisco Chronicle.


Shortly after noon on Friday, Su was reportedly traveling between 90 and 100 miles per hour when he struck the back of a stopped vehicle occupied by a two-year-old girl and her babysitter, an adult woman. Both were seriously injured and transported to a nearby hospital, where tragically the child later died despite lifesaving efforts.

Su suffered minor injuries, according to authorities. His charges have since been upgraded to murder and assault with a deadly weapon.

MacRumors today.

"Our hearts are broken by the tragic accident that happened outside of Apple Park Visitor Center," an Apple spokesperson said. "Our thoughts are with all of those grieving, and we are grateful for the care and support of the first responders."

The MacBook Air is our recommendation for most buyers. Both sizes offer a lightweight, silent laptop for everyday work, studying, and occasional creative projects. Choose the 13-inch for portability or the 15-inch for more workspace without MacBook Pro pricing.
We’d prioritize a competitive price on the memory and storage you need. For regular lengthy exports or other sustained demanding tasks, consider a MacBook Pro with active cooling instead.
U.S. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought the 13-inch M5 Air with 16GB memory and 512GB storage to $1,099, and the equivalent 15-inch to $1,299. Last Black Friday, the older M4 models with 256GB reached $749 and $949 respectively. We are already seeing up to $250 off the 1TB models, and $200 off the 512GB options, bringing the price back to the original MSRP before Apple increased prices.

Last Black Friday’s M4 models with 256GB reached £849 and £1,025. Match storage capacities when comparing generations. So far in November 2026 we are seeing the same £100 off the 13-inch MacBook Air, and £150 off the 15-inch model as we saw in Prime Day this October.

Eugen Wegmann




The MacBook Neo suits browsing, schoolwork, streaming, and office apps. Its lower starting price makes it appealing, but its fixed 8GB of memory leaves less room for demanding workloads.
Check which configuration is discounted: only the 512GB version includes Touch ID. Both lack a backlit keyboard, MagSafe, and Thunderbolt. Compare clearance MacBook Air stock before deciding how much those compromises save you.

Macbook Pro M6 Aufmacher

Halyna Kubiv




The standard M6 MacBook Pro is worth considering if you want a better built-in display, more connections, and cooling for sustained workloads without paying for a Pro or Max chip. It comes in a 14-inch size, with a non-touch Liquid Retina XDR display, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot.
It starts with 16GB memory and 1TB storage, so account for those specifications when comparing prices with an Air or older Pro. Despite the newer generation number, the standard M6 isn’t automatically the better choice for demanding work than an M5 Pro or M5 Max.

MacBook Pro M5 Pro – Best for demanding professional work

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The non-touchscreen M5 Pro MacBook Pro is a strong choice for development, photography, video editing, and heavier multitasking. Available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, it offers professional performance without the Max chip’s higher price.
Compare it with the touchscreen version using the same memory and storage. Both offer M5 Pro configurations, so a discounted non-touch model could be particularly good value if its existing XDR display meets your needs.

MacBook Pro M5 Max – Best for demanding graphics and video

				
					

				
			
Stephan Wiesend




Consider the non-touchscreen M5 Max MacBook Pro if your work benefits from additional graphics power or more memory than an M5 Pro supports. Complex 3D projects and demanding video production make a stronger case for it than everyday productivity.
We’d choose the configuration around the work you do. A larger advertised discount on a Max doesn’t necessarily make it better value than a less expensive Pro that meets your needs. Our MacBook Pro buying advice explains the options.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro – Best for its OLED display

				
					

				
			


Roman Loyola/Foundry




The touchscreen MacBook Pro is most compelling for its OLED display and thinner, lighter design. Improved blacks and reduced blooming could matter more to your everyday experience than touch controls, particularly if you spend most of your working day using the built-in screen.
Available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes with M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, these models offer comparable processing performance to their non-touch equivalents. Compare matching configurations: the regular premium is $400/£400, so consider how much you’ll benefit from the display before paying extra.

Should you buy a Mac or MacBook now or wait for a better deal?
With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need a Mac immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so an early offer can be worth taking if it matches or approaches a previous low for the same configuration. Waiting can be a gamble if you’re buying clearance stock with a particular screen size, memory capacity, or finish.
The M5 MacBook Air remains an appealing purchase at a good discount, with a replacement not expected until 2027. The recently updated Mac mini and Mac Studio are also worth considering if they meet your needs. The main reason to wait is a better price rather than an imminent replacement.
MacBook Pro buyers no longer need to wait for the rumored October launches: the standard M6 and OLED touchscreen models are now available. However, their recent arrival may limit initial discounts. Non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max models could offer better value, particularly if you don’t need the touchscreen version’s improved display and lighter design. If your existing M4 or M5 MacBook Pro still meets your needs, there’s little reason to upgrade simply because a newer option exists.
The M6 iMac has only just arrived, replacing the aging M4 version. Compare a modest saving on the latest model with a substantial clearance discount on its predecessor, rather than assuming the older machine is automatically the better deal.
Previous prices need context this year. Following June’s increases, a discount from Apple’s current asking price may still leave you paying more than before the increases. Compare retailers as well: Amazon competes with Best Buy, Walmart, and B&H in the U.S., and retailers including Currys and John Lewis in the U.K. Our MacBook Pro buying advice explains the current choices.


						

							


Which Mac specifications are worth paying for?
The cheapest Mac isn’t always the best value. Use Black Friday to get a configuration that will serve you for longer within your budget, but don’t pay for performance or features you won’t use.
Check the exact chip, screen size, memory, and storage. A standard M6 and an M5 Pro or M5 Max serve different needs: the newer generation number alone doesn’t tell you which is better for your work. For MacBook Pro listings, distinguish the OLED touchscreen version from non-touch models.
Avoid saving a small amount by buying too little memory or storage. Most current Macs start with 16GB of unified memory, but the MacBook Neo has a fixed 8GB, and some desktop configurations include only a 256GB SSD. Unified memory cannot be upgraded later. An external SSD can add storage, but it cannot compensate for insufficient RAM.
Once the processor meets your needs, additional memory may be more useful than a faster chip. Compare a discounted Air with the Neo, too: the M5 Air starts with twice the memory and storage of the entry-level Neo. Our Mac buying guide explains which specifications suit different workloads.
Check whether the configuration includes nano-texture glass. This optional finish reduces glare and reflections, which can help in bright rooms or near windows, but increases the price. If reflections rarely bother you, standard glass may offer better value.


						

							


Should you buy an older Mac or MacBook?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




An older Mac can be excellent value if its price reflects its age and configuration. Compare its actual selling price with the discounted price of the newer equivalent, rather than focusing on a large percentage saving from its original launch price.
Previous-generation Apple silicon models are the most promising starting point. A discounted M4 MacBook Air or standard M5 MacBook Pro may meet your needs comfortably. Older Pro and Max configurations can also be worth considering if they provide the memory, graphics performance, and connections your work requires for substantially less money.
Check what the saving buys—and what you give up. An older Mac with more memory or storage could be more useful than a newer entry-level configuration. Conversely, a cheaper older Air with 256GB storage isn’t directly comparable with an M5 Air that starts with 512GB. The non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros also remain current options, despite the arrival of the standard M6 and touchscreen models.
Be much more cautious with Intel Macs. Their software support is winding down, and a low purchase price may leave you with a machine that has a limited useful life for current apps and macOS features. Check compatibility with the software you need before buying any older model.
For used or refurbished Macs, check battery condition on laptops, warranty coverage, and the returns policy. Confirm that Activation Lock has been removed and that the Mac isn’t still enrolled in an organization’s management system.

Should I buy a MacBook Pro?
Should I buy a Mac mini?
Should I buy a Mac Studio?


						

							


Mac or MacBook deals to avoid
Treat large advertised discounts carefully. Following June’s price increases, “$400 off” may simply bring a Mac closer to what it cost before the increase. Compare previous selling prices for the same configuration, rather than judging the offer solely against today’s recommended price.
Check whether the price includes AppleCare+ or another protection plan. Some Amazon listings bundle coverage with the Mac. If you don’t want it, a listing without coverage could be cheaper; if you do, compare the bundle with buying the Mac and coverage separately.
Check for a bundled power adapter, too. Some Mac laptops are sold without one in the U.K. and EU. A charger bundle may be useful if you need an adapter, but could mean paying extra unnecessarily if you already own a suitable one.
Compare the complete setup cost. A Mac mini or Studio requires a display, keyboard, and mouse or trackpad, while adapters and docks can add to the cost of any Mac.
Finally, distinguish cash discounts from gift cards, trade-ins, financing, and membership-only offers. Read the conditions, check the seller, and confirm whether the Mac is new, refurbished, or used, along with its warranty and returns policy.


						

							


How we choose Mac and MacBook deals
Macworld has covered the Mac since its launch in 1984, and our recommendations draw on decades of experience and hands-on reviews. We consider performance, display quality, battery life, portability, connectivity, and everyday use alongside price to explain which Macs suit different buyers.
Our reviews help us assess which upgrades are worth paying for. We look at whether additional processing power benefits demanding workloads, when more memory is useful, and whether a premium display justifies the extra cost. A MacBook Air may offer better value for everyday work, while a Pro, Max, or Ultra configuration needs to earn its higher price through the work it enables.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous offers, matching the exact chip, screen size, memory, and storage. Following Apple’s June price increases, we also consider earlier selling prices rather than judging a deal solely against today’s recommended retail price. A large advertised discount doesn’t automatically make an offer exceptional.
We consider the complete purchase, too: the retailer, product condition, warranty, and any conditions attached to the price. For desktop Macs, we also account for the display and accessories you’ll need. Our Mac buying guide and MacBook comparison explain how to choose the right model and configuration.
For more offers, visit our Black Friday coverage and our roundups of the best iPad deals, AirPods deals, and Apple Watch deals.

title: Google Says Gemini App Rolling Out on Apple CarPlay Starting Today
content:
Google has announced that a dedicated Gemini app on Apple CarPlay is rolling out around the world in several languages starting today, allowing you to have conversations with the AI assistant right from your vehicle's dashboard.


Gemini conversations on your iPhone automatically sync to CarPlay, so you can continue a previous conversation or start a new one.

For example, you can ask Gemini to "Give me my daily brief for today" and it can give you a personalized answer based on your information in apps such as Gmail and Google Calendar. Or if you are driving around and looking for a restaurant, you could ask "What's a quick lunch spot in downtown Austin that's easy to get in and out of?"

To get started, make sure you have the latest version of the Gemini app on your iPhone. Then, tap on the Gemini icon on CarPlay to start a conversation.

CarPlay gained support for voice-based conversational AI apps starting with iOS 26.4. AI apps that have already rolled out CarPlay support include OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, X's Grok, Microsoft's Copilot, Perplexity, and others. iOS 27 also added Siri AI support to CarPlay, complete with a Siri app.

title: Is It Worth Buying a Ceramic Apple Watch?
content:
The Apple Watch Series 12's ceramic casing option is its most luxurious, offering a distinctive finish and highly scratch-resistant material at a price above both aluminum and titanium. Is it worth choosing?


The ceramic Apple Watch starts at $899, compared to $399 for aluminum and $699 for titanium. Available in Pearl White and Night Blue, it brings ceramic back to the lineup for the first time since the Series 5. It is aimed at buyers who want a more unusual and special Apple Watch, and are willing to pay for the material and appearance rather than additional features.

described a manufacturing process that combined zirconia powder with alumina before molding the case, heating it to form a dense solid, and polishing it with a diamond slurry. That process produced the smooth surface and rich white appearance that helped make the ceramic Apple Watch Edition so distinctive.

The included band is part of that appeal. Apple pairs the ceramic watches with exclusive Sand and Navy Blue Sport Bands featuring ceramic pin-and-tuck closures that match their respective cases. The Sand band gives the Pearl White model a distinctive overall appearance, with the matching ceramic closure providing a detail absent from ordinary Sport Bands.

Ceramic also offers a different look when paired with other bands. Pearl White creates a striking contrast with darker rubber or woven bands, while Night Blue offers a more understated combination. Metal bracelets remain an option, although their connectors will contrast with the ceramic case; buyers who prefer a coordinated metallic appearance may favor titanium with a Link Bracelet or Milanese Loop.

Ceramic also offers a practical benefit beyond its appearance: resistance to cosmetic wear. Earlier ceramic Apple Watch models were known for cases that were exceptionally difficult to scratch, helping preserve their finish throughout years of use. Polished titanium can pick up visible surface scratches, so buyers concerned about their watch retaining its original appearance have a good reason to consider ceramic.

Ceramic can still chip or crack under forceful impact, even though it resists scratches very well. It is a luxury case material with useful durability characteristics, rather than a substitute for the Apple Watch Ultra's rugged design.

Like titanium, the ceramic Series 12 features a sapphire front crystal that is highly resistant to scratches. Aluminum models instead feature Ceramic Shield 2, which refers to the front cover rather than a ceramic case. Titanium provides sapphire for $200 less, but it does not replicate the ceramic casing's distinctive finish or material qualities.

The ceramic models also include cellular connectivity as standard, while aluminum models offer a choice of GPS or GPS and Cellular. The $500 difference between their starting prices therefore covers more than the case material and front crystal, although ceramic remains a substantial premium even when comparing equivalent configurations.

larger and heavier than their aluminum and titanium counterparts, without providing a larger display. The larger ceramic model weighs 51.3 grams in Pearl White and 52.9 grams in Night Blue, compared to 44.9 grams for titanium.

Apple Watch Ultra 4, despite the Ultra offering longer battery life and additional capabilities.

Aluminum remains the stronger choice for buyers focused on features and value, while titanium offers a premium metallic finish and sapphire crystal at a lower price. Ceramic is for buyers who place greater importance on the material, finish, and sense of wearing something more unusual. If Pearl White is the Apple Watch you particularly want, neither titanium nor the Apple Watch Ultra offers a comparable substitute, regardless of their practical advantages.

content:
Maybe you used them to sound off, maybe you relied on fellow users to solve problems, and maybe, just maybe, Apple would answer questions on its support community forum. But no more.


You'll still be able to find answers as Apple Support Community's forums will remain searchable. But there's no more asking questions or connecting with other users - image credit: Apple.

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max Wins Battery Test Involving 32 Smartphones
content:
Apple's iPhone 18 Pro Max placed first overall in a battery comparison of 32 smartphones, with other iPhone models leading individual tests and matching significantly more expensive devices.


CNET assessed each phone using two tests totaling three hours and 45 minutes. One measured battery consumption during three hours of video streaming over Wi-Fi at maximum screen brightness. The other combined video playback, video calls, gaming, and social media use over 45 minutes. Both began at 100% charge, and the publication averaged the remaining percentages to produce its overall rankings.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max and Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, each finished the mixed-use test with 99% remaining, sharing first place. Google's Pixel 11 Pro XL retained 97%, improving on the Pixel 10 Pro XL's 93% result in the same test.

The smaller iPhone 18 Pro delivered the strongest result in the video streaming test, retaining 94% of its charge after three hours. The iPhone 17 also performed well across both benchmarks, alongside Motorola's Razr and Razr Ultra models.

CNET credited the iPhone 18 Pro Max's overall lead to a battery capacity increase over the iPhone 17 Pro Max, combined with the A20 Pro chip's efficiency and iOS 27 optimizations.

Despite sharing first place in the mixed-use test, the $1,999 iPhone Duo tied for fourth overall. Its combined result matched the $699 iPhone 17e and $1,400 Motorola Razr Ultra, putting the less expensive iPhone alongside two foldable devices costing substantially more.

CNET's comparison of average results by manufacturer for the second consecutive year. Only brands represented by multiple tested models were included, with OnePlus finishing second.

CNET, phones tested in 2026 had approximately the same average battery performance as those tested in 2025 and 2024. Larger batteries do not necessarily translate into longer use between charges, since displays, processors, and other features also affect power consumption.

title: Apple suddenly shutters its Support Community forums for no clear reason
content:
Macworld





If you’ve ever had a problem with an Apple product and looked online for a solution, there’s a high probability you’ve ended up on the Support Community forums. This is a site owned and operated by Apple, but reliant on the expertise of members of the public, who start threads about ongoing issues (such as the iPhone Duo’s cracked screens) and offer each other advice. You won’t always be able to find a perfect fix there, but it’s a great place to find confirmation that other people are experiencing the same issue as you, and to keep track of the best workarounds currently available.
Sadly, however, the site’s days are officially numbered. At the time of writing, visitors are greeted by a message announcing that Apple Support Community “will permanently close on November 20, 2026,” and directing those seeking guidance to instead head over to Apple’s Support site. (The company also offers support via phone, chat, face to face in stores, and through the Apple Support app.) For the time being, existing community threads are still available to view, but nothing further can be added. The forums are read-only from now on, and the entire thing will close down in nine days.
Apple doesn’t offer a reason for the decision in its announcement. We asked the company what was going on, and received a statement saying only that it evaluated its strategy and customers’ needs and then decided to close the forums. No details were offered as to how the forums’ existence clashed with strategy, nor in what way it was a bad thing for customers to have access to a repository of advice and guidance from fellow Apple fans. So we can only speculate about the rationale.

				
					

				
			
Apple




One obvious issue with the forums would be the same one encountered by every company operating such a site: The owner has responsibility for the content without having control over it. If news of a hardware problem breaks, forum users will discuss it in a way that carries consequences for Apple’s corporate strategy, potentially widening awareness before the company is ready to release a statement or even seeding misinformation, and disgruntled device owners are unlikely to follow Apple’s desired messaging lines when complaining about the latest thing that has gone wrong. In the thread I linked above, for example, several commenters point out that the screen issue is rare and covered by warranty, but another advises the thread author to stick with conventional iPhones and avoid the Duo for now.
In other words, Apple probably didn’t like the idea of owners googling a problem with their device, seeing the forums in a prominent search ranking and with official Apple branding, and then being exposed to unofficial messaging. It’s a company which is notorious for wanting to control the narrative at all times, and forums are a terrible medium for that.
On the other hand, forums are a brilliant way to generate large amounts of content without having to pay for it, and Apple is about to kiss that goodbye. Apple’s community forums have been around for decades, dating all the way back to 1998. Longtime Apple users will fondly recall browsing Apple Discussion threads before Reddit or Discord were a thing.
In the vacuum left by Support Community’s absence, users will have to look elsewhere. Other sites may see an increase in traffic to their own forums (and Apple will have even less control over the discussions on there) while others with a preference for the official route will visit Apple Support.
But a site curated by in-house writers, even one funded by a multi-trillionaire company like Apple, cannot possibly react as quickly to breaking stories and emerging vulnerabilities as a forum open to the public; it’s not just about manpower, but also about having to get clearance from the PR and legal departments before publishing anything. Apple Support is a more reliable resource in most respects than Support Community, but it cannot perform exactly the same function… unless John Ternus has an AI-based approach in mind.
We’ll have to wait and see what Apple’s support functions look like after this change. In the meantime, make the most of Support Community while you still can.
creator: Macworld
