title: The new MacBook Pro has a brilliant cooling system
content:
Macworld





The more we learn about Apple’s new MacBook Pro, the more we see how different the design is. There’s the display, which has some of the best specs we’ve ever seen; the speakers, which generate more bass when the lid is closed; and the hinge, which is more stable to accommodate taps and pinches. And now we’ve gotten a look at the cooling, which might be the most beautiful of all.
In its announcement of the MacBook Pro, Apple called out its “completely redesigned thermal architecture,” which “enables the same incredible sustained performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, even in a lighter design, while redirecting warm air away from the display.” That sounds like a lot of fancy words for a whole lot of nothing, but it turns out it’s actually completely reimagined.
A YouTube video by Geekerwan compared the mini-LED MacBook Pro with the new PROLED XDR model using a fog machine. With each MacBook’s fans running, you can clearly see how the internal design disperses the heat: In the old model, heat goes both out and up through the display, while the PROLED pushes the heat toward the back of the device through the hinge.

				
					

				
			As you can see in this image, the new MacBook Pro, right, disperses heat out through the hinge rather than up through the display.

Geekerwan /YouTube




Pushing the heat out the back is no easy task and required a thorough redesign of the hinge and ventilation system. Not only does the new MacBook Pro do a better job of keeping heat away from the keyboard and display, as Geekerwan explains, but the benefit isn’t simply better cooling capacity when working on the PROLED screen. It also helps disperse heat better when the lid is closed and hooked up to an external monitor. To drive the point home, he tested both models closed and found a massive drop in performance on the older model as a result of thermal throttling.
Geekerwan also found that the fans spun faster and were quieter on the PROLED model. It’s unclear whether that’s due to new hardware or software tweaks, but iFixit’s teardown found the same fan placement under the logic board and nothing particularly noteworthy about the fans themselves.
Check out our 5-star review of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.
creator: Macworld

title: The iPhone 18 Pro has one job: Keep selling Duos
content:
Macworld





When the iPhone 18 Pro was announced in September, it was only part of the story of this year’s flagship iPhones. On paper, the 18 Pro is faster, has a better camera, and features a more efficient vapor chamber — all small improvements that enhance the user experience — but together, a very small upgrade to the iPhone 17 Pro. 




That’s no surprise, since the star of the show this year isn’t the iPhone 18 Pro, but the iPhone Duo. And the more I think about Apple’s 2026 lineup, the more it reminds me of another very important year for the iPhone: 2017.
Back when Apple introduced the iPhone X in 2017, it represented the future of the iPhone. It ditched the Home button in favor of an edge-to-edge display. Touch ID was replaced by Face ID. It was a completely new concept for the iPhone — yet it was too expensive by 2017 standards. It was the first iPhone to hit the market with a price tag of $999, several hundred dollars more than any other iPhone. 
To cushion the blow, Apple also offered the iPhone 8 and iPhone 8 Plus. Those phones were good — easily the best iteration of that classic iPhone design with a faster chip, better cameras, and a new glass back with wireless charging. But compared to the iPhone X, they weren’t exactly an exciting upgrade. And that was the point.
iPhone X redux
Back in 2017, if you wanted a new iPhone, didn’t really care about the new design, and didn’t want to spend more than you ever did on an iPhone, you bought the iPhone 8. If you were an enthusiast and wanted to experience with what the future of the iPhone looked like, you’d buy an iPhone X. 
Nearly a decade later, Apple is doing something similar. The iPhone 18 Pro is the safe choice, while iPhone Duo is the experiment.

				
					

				
			
The iPhone 8, right, merely existed to make the iPhone X more desireable.

Foundry




But the reality is, most people don’t buy new iPhones every year. Apple itself told me that many customers keep the same iPhone for about three years — something many reviewers don’t take into account when talking about a new iPhone. For Apple, someone buying an iPhone 18 Pro is likely upgrading from an iPhone 15 Pro. That means three years’ worth of improvements in the camera, battery life, and a few design changes — all at once. It’s a big leap.
That said, the iPhone 18 Pro serves a second purpose in this year’s lineup. It’s not just the iPhone that looks familiar — it’s also the one that makes the iPhone Duo feel that much more exciting. For many tech enthusiasts like me, the excitement over the iPhone 18 Pro fades within minutes of setting up the new phone. The iPhone Duo, on the other hand, brings a whole new experience to the iPhone. 
So when you go to Apple’s website to decide which new phone to buy, it’s not hard to imagine which one seems more appealing. One looks just like last year’s phone and the other is a completely new thing.
Who the iPhone 18 Pro is really for
For people who really want the feeling of having something new, they’ll look at both new iPhones and will certainly consider buying the iPhone Duo. If you’ve spent the past few years complaining that every new iPhone is essentially the same, Apple finally has something very different for you. 
That’s basically the same choice Apple gave customers in 2017. The iPhone 8 made the iPhone X seem like a much more exciting upgrade for enthusiasts — the iPhone Duo now fills that role.
And like the iPhone X, the iPhone Duo is expensive. So is the iPhone 18 Pro, though. It starts at $1,200 and gets close to $2,000 once you move up to the Pro Max and add storage. But put it next to the iPhone Duo, and it suddenly doesn’t feel so expensive anymore. 
Almost a decade ago, the iPhone 8 was the iPhone most people went to Apple Stores to buy. But once they got there, more than a few ended up choosing the iPhone X instead. This year, the iPhone 18 Pro is in the same position and is likely to have a similar effect with the Duo. The “boring” iPhone might be just the thing Apple needs to keep its super-expensive next-gen iPhone flying off shelves.

title: Best Virtual Machine Software for Mac (2026): Compare Parallels, VMware Fusion, UTM & more
content:
Macworld





Even the most loyal Mac users recognize that Windows still rules the roost in the world of desktop and laptop computers, and there are many important apps that only run on Windows. For example, the Windows version of Microsoft Office includes the Access database that has never been available for the Mac, and there are many professional graphics and video tools that are Windows-only. And, of course, there are all those A-List games that have never even glanced in the direction of us poor, forgotten Mac gamers.
If you need to run Windows software or games on your Macs then this article will reveal the best way to do so. 
Read on to discover the best options for running Windows, and Windows apps, on your Mac. You may also like to read our guide to How to install Windows and run Windows apps on a Mac (M-series models). We also cover how to run Windows on an Intel Mac separately.
Best Virtual Machine for Mac 2026: Best VMs to run Windows on a Mac
Read on for the best virtual machines for Mac. Our top choice is Parallels, now version 27, but we also consider VMware and alternative options, including emulators that let you run Windows apps on a Mac without even installing Windows to Microsoft’s Windows 365 service.
At a Glance Best VM Comparison


ToolBest ForPriceApple Silicon Support

Parallels DesktopBest overallPaidYes
VMware FusionFree personal useFreeYes
CrossOverWindows apps w/o WindowsPaidYes
UTMBest for open-source developersFree/$9.99Yes

 



		

			

				
					

				
								
Pros
Straightforward Windows installation.
Excellent integration with Mac apps.
Useful tools for development and testing.
Improved graphics support for professional software.
										
Cons
Most editions require a subscription.
Windows licensing costs extra.
Version 27 requires Apple silicon.
Limited compatibility with modern Windows games.

Parallels Desktop remains our top choice for running Windows alongside macOS. It creates a virtual PC on your Mac, letting you use Windows applications without restarting. You can also create Linux and macOS virtual machines for development and testing.
Its biggest strength is how comfortably Windows fits into a Mac workflow. Coherence mode hides the Windows desktop, leaving individual Windows apps alongside your Mac apps. You can keep Windows applications in the Dock, share folders, copy and paste between applications, and drag files between operating systems.
Parallels can download and install Windows 11 on Arm for you. You’ll need a suitable Windows licence, although an eligible existing key may save you buying another.
Version 27 supports macOS 27 Golden Gate and drops support for Intel Macs, whose owners must use an earlier release. Its main addition is OpenGL 4.3 support for demanding Windows graphics applications, with full hardware acceleration requiring an M3 or newer Mac running macOS Sequoia or later.
Standard suits everyday Windows applications, while Pro offers higher resource limits and additional developer tools. Standard has subscription and one-time purchase options; Pro requires a subscription. Major upgrades are included while a subscription is active.
Allow plenty of memory: 16GB or more is recommended. Gaming remains a weakness, with DirectX 11.1 support leaving many DirectX 12 titles out of reach. Use the 14-day trial to check your essential software.
For regular Windows work, Parallels’ ease of use and close Mac integration justify its place ahead of the alternatives.

			

				
					

				
								
Pros
Fusion allows you to use it for free if it’s for personal, home and student use.
										
Cons
VMware doesn’t update Fusion as regularly as Parallels is updated.
									
Retailer
					
Price
					
VMware (Fusion Player, personal use)
											
Free					
View Deal					
VMware Fusion Pro (non-commercial use)
											
Free					
View Deal					
VMware Desktop Hypervisor Pro
											
$120					
View Deal					
For many years, VMware Fusion and Parallels Desktop competed head-to-head as the leading virtualization software for Mac, with both companies regularly updating their software with new features and performance improvements. In recent years, however, VMware has slowed development, and Fusion no longer receives the same level of attention. In fact, the software has become surprisingly difficult to find on VMware’s website since Broadcom acquired the company.
Fusion 13, released in November 2022, added support for virtualization on Apple Silicon Macs, allowing M1 and M2 users to run the Arm version of Windows. Like Parallels Desktop, Fusion virtualizes Windows on Arm on Apple silicon Macs. Parallels also offers limited emulation of Intel-based operating systems in its Pro, Business and Enterprise editions, but performance is slow and significant restrictions apply.
Subsequent updates addressed some of these shortcomings. Fusion 13.5, released in October 2023, introduced DirectX 11 support for improved graphics performance and added a Get Windows option that simplified downloading and installing Windows 11 on Arm. Version 13.6 followed in September 2024 with vmcli command-line support and compatibility with newer guest operating systems, although the pace of development still lagged behind Parallels.
One of Fusion’s biggest advantages is its price. VMware first introduced a free personal edition with Fusion Player in 2020, but it now offers the full-featured Fusion Pro free for personal, home and student use. After creating a VMware account, users can download the software without paying a licence fee, making it one of the best-value virtualization solutions available.
Like Parallels, Fusion creates a virtual machine that lets you run Windows, Linux and other operating systems alongside macOS without rebooting. It supports Intel and Apple Silicon Macs, allows users to customise CPU and memory allocation, create snapshots, drag and drop files between operating systems and accelerate graphics using DirectX 11.
However, Fusion no longer matches Parallels for ease of use. Downloading the software still involves navigating Broadcom’s confusing website, and while the Get Windows feature has simplified installation, the overall setup process remains more technical than Parallels. Fusion has also dropped its Unity mode, which previously integrated Windows applications directly into the macOS desktop, and it still lacks DirectX 12 support, limiting compatibility with many modern games.
Although VMware Fusion has fallen behind its main rival in polish and new features, its strong performance and free personal licence make it an excellent choice for developers, IT professionals, students and home users who occasionally need to run Windows on a Mac. Users looking for the smoothest, most beginner-friendly experience, however, will still find Parallels Desktop the better all-round option.
You’ll need to register for a VMware account, but Fusion Pro is free to download here.

			

				
					

				
								
Pros
Affordable/free option for running Windows on Mac
Runs on Intel and Apple Silicon
Runs older versions of Windows and Linux
										
Cons
More complex than its rivals
No tech-support
									
Retailer
					
Price
					
Mac App Store
											
$9.99					
View Deal					
UTM Virtual Machines from Turing Software is currently sitting at no.1 on the Business section of the Mac App Store. It costs $9.99/£9.99 on the Mac App Store, but, because UTM is an open-source project, there’s also a free version–simply called UTM–available on the Turing website.
UTM can run on Macs with either Intel or Apple Silicon processors (running macOS Big Sur 11.3 or later). It provides two different options depending on the type of Mac you’re using–virtualization and emulation.
So, if you have an Intel Mac, UTM can use virtualization to create a virtual machine that runs the Intel version of Windows. And, if you have a Mac with Apple Silicon you can use virtualization to create a virtual machine that runs Windows On Arm. But, if you want to run the older Intel version of Windows on a Mac with Apple Silicon, then UTM will use emulation in order to run Window since that version isn’t designed for the Mac processors. Virtualization provides better performance, but emulation is useful if you need to run Windows apps or software that require a specific version of Windows.
UTM’s combination of virtualization and emulation makes it useful for running different operating systems and processor architectures. Parallels also offers limited x86 emulation, but its main strength is running Arm-based virtual machines on Apple silicon. UTM requires more technical knowledge: expect to work with installation images and configure settings yourself, with less guidance than Parallels provides.
Performance is good, though. The one weakness is that UTM offers experimental Windows 11 3D graphics acceleration, although game compatibility is limited and instability is possible. But if you just want to run business apps or check out the new AI features in Windows, then UTM is a good, low-cost option that will appeal to developers and technical users.

			

				
					

				
								
Pros
14-day trial
Doesn’t require a full version of Windows
Improved interface and ease of use
Regular updates, good technical support
										
Cons
Some Windows apps aren’t compatible
Can be complicated to use
Requires Rosetta on Apple Silicon
									
Retailer
					
Price

$74					
View Deal					
CrossOver is one of the easiest ways to run Windows software on a Mac without buying or installing Windows itself. Built on the open-source WINE compatibility layer, it translates Windows API calls into macOS equivalents, allowing many Windows apps and games to run natively rather than through a virtual machine.
Unlike Parallels Desktop or VMware Fusion, CrossOver doesn’t require a Windows licence, making it a lighter and more affordable option. CodeWeavers has also added a polished interface, technical support and installation tools that make it far easier to use than WINE itself.
CrossOver’s biggest strength is gaming. Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit is based on CodeWeavers technology, and regular updates continue to improve compatibility with popular titles. Recent releases have added or enhanced support for games including Diablo IV, Path of Exile 2, Kingdom Come: Deliverance II, The Outer Worlds 2 and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. It also handles many productivity applications and older Windows programs surprisingly well.
Compatibility is still its biggest limitation. Some applications work flawlessly, others have minor glitches, and some won’t run at all. Fortunately, CodeWeavers provides an online compatibility database, and the generous 14-day free trial lets you test your essential software before buying.
Performance on Apple Silicon Macs remains good despite the current version relying on Apple’s Rosetta translation layer. That should improve significantly with CrossOver 27, expected in early 2027, which will run natively on Apple Silicon as Apple will retire Rosetta. The trade-off is that CrossOver 27 will drop support for Intel-based Macs, although existing users can continue using older versions.
CrossOver 26 and its subsequent 26.1 and 26.3 updates have focused on performance improvements, Wine 11.0, better graphics support through D3DMetal 3.0, interface refinements for macOS Tahoe, bug fixes and expanded game compatibility.
At $74/£60 for a a licence including one year of updates and support (or $494/£414 for a lifetime licence), CrossOver isn’t free, but it’s still considerably cheaper than buying Windows and virtualisation software.
CrossOver isn’t perfect, but if you want to run Windows software or games on a Mac without installing Windows, it’s one of the best and most convenient solutions available.

			

				
					

				
								
Pros
Can run Windows on your Mac and also your iPad or iPhone. 
										
Cons
Needs a fast – and always on – Internet connection. 
Expensive.
									
Retailer
					
Price
					
$31					
View Deal					
Windows 365 (which launched in July 2021) has the potential to really challenge traditional virtualization programs such as Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion. However, at the moment, Windows 365 is still pretty expensive and is very much aimed at large corporate users, rather than the individuals and smaller businesses that tend to use Parallels and Fusion.
Microsoft describes Windows 365 as a Cloud PC, but its technical notes make it clear that Windows 365 is a form of virtual machine. The difference is that Parallels and Fusion create virtual machines that are stored locally on your Mac itself, and these virtual machines rely on your Mac’s own processor power, memory and storage to run Windows and Windows apps.
In contrast, Windows 365 creates a virtual machine that is stored up in the cloud, and runs on Microsoft’s own servers. The video image for the Windows desktop on your cloud PC is then streamed to your Mac – or any other device, such as an iPad or even another Windows PC – via your broadband connection.
This form of virtual machine can work well, as long as you have a fast enough – and always-on – Internet connection. But, as mentioned, Windows 365 is quite expensive, with prices ranging from $31/£26.40 to $66/£56.20 per month. Parallels Desktop Standard offers annual subscription and one-time purchase options, although Windows licensing is separate.
Windows 365 certainly has appeal to larger businesses that want to provide a standardized cloud PC that their staff can connect to from any location that has an Internet connection – it’s ideal for hybrid working and the ‘new normal’. However, it’s too expensive for ordinary home users, students and smaller businesses, so existing users of Parallels and Fusion will probably want to stick with those apps for the time being.
Read more here: 
How to use Windows 365 on Mac, iPad and iPhone.

			

				
					

				
								
Pros
Free.
										
Cons
Not really for beginners. 
									
Retailer
					
Price
					
Wine
											
Free					
View Deal					
As we mentioned above, the third technology option – after Boot Camp and virtualization – is Wine, which allows you to run Windows apps without Windows itself.
If you don’t mind rolling up your sleeves and getting your hands a bit dirty, then Wine is an unusual but feasible option for running Windows software on your Mac.
Like VirtualBox, Wine is an open-source program that you can download for free. However, it doesn’t use conventional virtualization technology to create a virtual machine for installing Windows – in fact, Wine is the only program in this group that doesn’t even require a copy of Windows at all.
Instead, Wine acts as a kind of software middleman that translates the programming routines – called APIs – in Windows apps so that they can talk directly to macOS, without needing a full copy of Windows itself. And as you don’t need a lot of extra memory or processor power in order to run Windows, you may find that Wine can actually provide better performance than using a virtual machine (especially for games and graphics apps).
Wine also gets very regular updates from a team of dedicated developers who provide the software for free.
The downside is that Wine can be spectacularly confusing for beginners – to the point where we can only really recommend it to hobbyists who like a bit of a challenge.
CodeWeavers CrossOver for Mac is a little easier to use than Wine, despite being closely related to the software. But of course Wine is free, which is a big bonus.

			

				
					

				
								
Pros
Free for personal/educational use.
										
Cons
Very complicated, not for beginners
									
Retailer
					
Price
					
Oracle
											
Free					
View Deal					
This open-source virtualization program is free for personal use – but it’s more at home in a corporate environment.
VirtualBox is a bit of a mixed bag. Like Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion, it allows you to create a virtual machine that can run Windows and Windows apps from within macOS itself. You’ll need to purchase a Windows license for installation and a special version of Windows, Windows On ARM, for Apple Silicon Macs. 
If you want it for personal or educational use then VirtualBox is free. The disadvantage of open-source software is that VirtualBox isn’t as polished or easy to use as Parallels or Fusion. As the program is free, you also don’t get any technical support and the 200-page manual is designed for IT managers and developers, making even simple tasks like changing the virtual machine window resolution baffling. 
Luckily there is a busy user forum where you can ask a few questions when you need to. Which is a good thing because VirtualBox throws a lot of jargon at you and if you don’t know the difference between a virtual hard disk and a virtual machine disk then you might find it a bit tricky to get started.
Version 7.1 did introduce a new StartUp Wizard to simplify the setup process with separate ‘Basic’ and ‘Expert’ modes. However, this only partially addresses the program’s complex interface, and creating a Windows VM from a Windows 11 On ARM disk image on our M2 MacBook Pro took several attempts.
Version 7.1 also added support for Apple Silicon (aka M-series Macs). The support for Apple Silicon is limited though. VirtualBox can run Windows VMs in its own window or in ‘Seamless’ mode, where individual Windows apps run as native Mac apps. However, we found apps in Seamless mode sometimes move around on the screen, leaving odd graphical after-images. We also experienced occasional crashes when shutting down the Windows VM.
VirtualBox’s base package is free for personal, educational and commercial use. Businesses only need a paid commercial licence if they use the optional Oracle Extension Pack, which adds extra features. Oracle also offers paid enterprise support.

			

				
					

				
								
Pros
Windows can run at full speed because its not being run at the same time as macOS.
										
Cons
Intel only. Absent from M-series Macs. 
You can’t run Windows and macOS at the same time.
No official Windows 11 support.
									
Using dual-boot rather than virtualization technology, Boot Camp provides the best performance for Intel-based Macs that need to run Windows. (As we explained above, M1 or later Macs do not offer Boot Camp).
However, Apple officially supports Windows 10 through Boot Camp, and standard Windows 10 support ended on October 14, 2025. Continued security updates require enrolment in Microsoft’s Extended Security Updates programme or another applicable support arrangement.
It’s important to make a distinction between Boot Camp and the virtualization programs that we look at here, such as Parallels Desktop, VMware Fusion and VirtualBox. Instead of creating a virtual machine that allows you to run Mac and Windows apps together at the same time, Boot Camp is a dual-boot system that simply allows you to boot (start) your Mac using either the native macOS or Windows (but not both at the same time).
Thanks to Boot Camp your Mac can act as a straightforward Windows PC, and devote all its processor power and memory to running Windows and your Windows apps. And, crucially, if your Mac has a decent graphics card, it can use the full power of the graphics card to help run your Windows software. That’s definitely the best option for people who need to run high-end graphics software or 3D games, as you get much better performance than when running Windows in a virtual machine.
The disadvantage of using Boot Camp is that you lose access to all your Mac apps while you’re running Windows. If you use Apple Mail for your emails then you’ll need to shut down Windows and Boot Camp, and switch back to macOS every time you want to send or receive an email. And, if truth be told, the current version of BootCamp 6.1 isn’t quite as straightforward to set up as it used to be.
Previous versions of Boot Camp did all the work for you – they would partition your hard drive, install Windows from a normal installer disk, and also install any driver software that you needed so that components such as your graphics card, keyboard and mouse all worked properly within Windows.
Boot Camp does not officially support Windows 11. Running Windows 11 in a virtual machine is a separate option: Parallels Desktop 27 requires Apple silicon, while Intel Mac owners need an earlier compatible release, such as Parallels Desktop 26.
You can’t install Windows from an old installer disk anymore either, so you’ll either have to download a disk image file for Windows – called an ISO file – from Microsoft’s own website, or use your Windows disk to create one. Boot Camp includes driver software for setting up Windows 8 and Windows 10, but if you’re a fan of Windows 7 (which some people prefer for gaming) then you’ll have to hunt around on Apple’s website for the drivers you need and make sure you follow the correct procedure when copying them on to your Boot Camp partition.
Still, if you persevere with all that, you will eventually have Windows running at full speed on your Mac, giving you access to a wide range of Windows software and games that require more power and speed than you can get from using virtual machine technology. Just as long as you don’t have an M1 Mac…
For more advice about accessories and software for your Mac, iPad or iPhone see all our Best Picks.
How to run Windows on Mac: Apple Silicon vs Intel 
If you are still using an Intel-based Mac you can use Apple’s Boot Camp to run Windows. However, in 2020 Apple started using its own processors that are based on Arm architecture rather than the x86 architecture used by Intel. Now every Mac Apple sells has an Apple-made M-series processor. Boot Camp is not available on M-series Macs.
That doesn’t mean that M-series Macs can no longer run Windows, it just means they can’t use Boot Camp and they need the Arm version of Windows. 
If you want to run Windows on an M-series Mac. You can choose from virtualization options like Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion, or compatibility layers like CrossOver and Wine, and even Microsoft’s Windows 365 service. You can read about all of these choices in our group test below as well as our individual reviews.
Our top choice is Parallels Desktop, but all the others have some benefits that may suit you. For example, CrossOver doesn’t actually need a copy of Windows to run Windows apps, and there are even free options like Wine.
What are Apple’s Virtualization.framework tools?
Apple’s Virtualization.framework is a native macOS framework introduced by Apple that lets developers create and manage virtual machines without relying on third-party hypervisors like Parallels or VMware. Unlike Parallels Desktop, it’s not an end-user application. Instead, it’s a set of APIs that developers use to build virtualization software. 
VirtualBuddy, a free open-source app for running macOS and Linux VMs is built on Apple’s Virtualization.framework. Other similar options include Tart and OrbStack. These tools are aimed at developers rather than consumers. 
Virtualization.framework offers some advantages that developers appreciate, including: 
Native support from Apple.
Lower resource overhead. 
Integration with macOS security features
However, there are limitations compared to running Parallels and other apps. 
 FAQ 


1.
What is a Virtual Machine?
Virtualization programs such as Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion run on the macOS, but allow you to create a Virtual Machine (or VM) that mimics the hardware of a Windows PC. This makes it possible to create a VM on your Mac and then install Windows – or another operating system, such as Linux – on the VM. This is a great solution as it allows you to run the Windows apps that you need right alongside your main Mac apps as well. The only disadvantage is that you need a pretty fast Mac with plenty of memory and storage to run Windows as a VM, since it means that your Mac is effectively running two operating systems at the same time.





2.
What is emulation?
Emulation is a process that allows individual Windows applications to run on a Mac without the need for the Windows operating system to be installed. This is achieved through emulation tools, such as Wine and CrossOver, which are typically used by technically proficient users.





3.
Do I need a Windows license?
It depends on which of those two methods you are using. If you are running Windows in a VM then you need a license in order to create a Windows VM on Macs with Apple Silicon processors, and, unfortunately, the less expensive Home edition isn’t supported. However, it is possible to use an existing Windows license if you have one and Microsoft doesn’t differentiate between Windows On Intel and Windows On Arm, see Parallel’s website here.
If you are using emulation you won’t need a copy of Windows.





4.
How can I get the Arm version of Windows
Parallels Desktop can download and install Windows 11 on Arm for your Apple silicon Mac.
In Parallels Control Center, click +, choose Get Windows 11 from Microsoft, then follow the installation prompts. Once Windows is installed, open Settings > System > Activation to activate it with an eligible existing Windows 11 Pro key or purchase a licence.
Windows licensing is separate from Parallels. You don’t need a special Arm product key, but each Windows installation needs its own valid licence.
Read our full Parallels Desktop review for more information.





5.
How do I run the X86 version of Windows on a Mac
On Apple silicon Macs, the usual approach is to run Windows 11 on Arm, which can run many applications originally written for Intel PCs.
If you need an entire Intel-based Windows environment, Parallels offers an x86 emulator in its Pro, Business and Enterprise editions. Introduced in version 20.2, it has substantial limitations, including slow performance, a single virtual CPU, an 8GB memory limit and no sound or USB support. UTM is another emulation option.
Intel Mac owners need virtualization software compatible with their hardware. Parallels Desktop 27 requires Apple silicon; version 26 remains an option for supported Intel Macs.





6.
Can I run Windows 11 on a Mac using VM software?
You can run Windows 11 on a Mac using virtual machine (VM) software. This method allows you to run Windows and its applications alongside macOS without needing to reboot your computer.
If your Mac has an M-series chip it use ARM-based processors and requires the ARM version of Windows 11, officially called Windows on ARM (WoA) or Windows 11 Arm64. You cannot run the standard Intel (x86) version of Windows on these Macs through virtualization without significant performance loss via emulation. 
A popular solution for accessing Windows-exclusive software, games, or development tools on a Mac is to create a “virtual machine” on your Mac, which is software that simulates the hardware of a PC. You can then install Windows 11 on this VM. 
To run Windows 11 in a VM, your Mac needs to be powerful enough to run two operating systems simultaneously. This means having sufficient memory (RAM), storage space, and processor power. a machine with at least 16GB of RAM is recommended for a smooth experience. 





7.
Which Virtual Machine app is best for developers?
Parallels Desktop remains our leading choice for developers who want straightforward setup, close macOS integration and flexible virtual-machine controls. Pro adds higher resource limits, command-line management and advanced networking tools.
Version 27 requires Apple silicon. Check your workflow before buying: nested virtualization, Hyper-V and WSL2 are unavailable in its Windows environment on Apple silicon.
UTM and VMware Fusion are alternatives worth considering, particularly if cost or support for other operating systems and architectures matters more than ease of use.

title: Make Apple Watch Listen for Sounds Like the Doorbell
content:
One of Apple's accessibility features on iPhone can listen for important sounds around you, such as a doorbell, siren or alarm, and it sends you a notification when it hears one. The feature has been extended to Apple's new Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 models, so the alert reaches your wrist even when your iPhone isn't with you.


It's especially useful for people who are deaf or hard of hearing, but it has everyday uses too. If you wear noise-cancelling headphones while working and don't want to miss the doorbell – if you're expecting a delivery, for example – your Apple Watch can alert you.

Sounds Your Apple Watch Can Detect

Sound Recognition can detect the following 15 sounds. Any you switch on in the iPhone's Sounds list are also detected by your Apple Watch when "Detect using Apple Watch" is enabled:

Fire Alarm

Siren

Smoke Alarm

Cat

Dog

Appliances

Car Horn

Doorbell

Door Knock

Glass Breaking

Kettle

Water Running

Baby Crying

Coughing

Shouting

If a sound isn't recognized automatically, you can also teach your iPhone a Custom Alarm or Custom Appliance or Doorbell from the same Sounds list.

What You'll Need

You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4 paired with an iPhone 11 or later, or an iPhone SE (2nd generation or later), running iOS 27. If you already use Sound Recognition on your iPhone, it turns on automatically for your Apple Watch, so you may not need to do anything. Either way, here's how to set it up:

Open the Settings app on your iPhone and tap Accessibility.

In the "Hearing" section, tap Sound & Name Recognition.

Tap Sound Recognition and turn on the Sound Recognition toggle, then turn on Detect using Apple Watch.
Tap Sounds and turn on the sounds you want to hear about, such as Doorbell. You can also choose a specific alert tone for each sound.

Apple says Sound Recognition is processed on your Apple Watch and iPhone and doesn't record or store audio. It shouldn't be treated as a safety system, though. You shouldn't rely on it in situations where you may be harmed or injured, in high-risk or emergency situations, or for navigation, per Apple's guidelines.

title: 'Apple Support Community' Permanently Closing on November 20
content:
Apple today announced that the long-running Apple Support Community discussion forums will be permanently closing on Friday, November 20. 


Effectively immediately, the Apple Support Community forums are in a read-only state, with new posts no longer being accepted. The final message posted to the site appears to have been submitted at 5:49 p.m. Pacific Time today.

There is still a sign-in button, but it leads to an internal portal for Apple's corporate employees.

The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

Apple Support site. 

It is the end of an era. Apple offered an online discussion forum for user-to-user technical support since 1998, when it launched the Apple Tech Exchange. The forums were renamed to Apple Discussions in 2000, and then to the Apple Support Communities in 2011, before taking on their current Apple Support Community name in 2022.

Some people are susceptible to potentially serious health issues from those strobing lights. Others may have existing health conditions that are aggravated by the flashing lights.

title: Apple's Claris Testing 'Harbor' App for Local AI on Macs
content:
Apple's Claris subsidiary is testing an app called Harbor, which turns Apple silicon Macs into a private AI server.


Harbor works with a single Apple silicon Mac, but it also supports connecting multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory for larger models. Apple added RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 with macOS Tahoe 26.2, making clustering faster.

Harbor detects devices connected over Thunderbolt 5 and lets users browse for, download, and load open-weight models. It's described as an easy-to-use app with no manual configuration required.
Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency than a single computer can handle alone.

Set up in minutes, not hours. Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you're running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.


Download and run models directly. Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.


Harbor is in early access and is not publicly available. There was an App Store listing, but it has now been removed.

Claris is known for its database platform FileMaker, which is aimed at businesses, so it isn't clear how Apple will market the Harbor app or whether it will be free. The sign-up page for Harbor asks for a company name, which suggests more of a business focus.

PRICES CHECKED 10 NOVEMBER 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November
Black Friday is a great time to buy an iPad, with discounts spanning affordable everyday tablets, powerful Pro models, and clearance stock from previous generations. Last year’s U.S. offers included $150 off the M3 iPad Air, $100 off the A17 Pro iPad mini, and $100 off the then-new M5 iPad Pro. The standard A16 iPad also briefly reached $279. In the U.K., highlights included £100 off the iPad Air, £50 off the mini, and substantial savings on older M4 iPad Pro models.
October Prime Day brought further discounts, although Apple’s June price increases made the advertised savings less straightforward. In the U.S., the 128GB A16 iPad was $399, the 128GB A17 Pro mini was $499, and the 11-inch M4 iPad Air with 128GB was $649. U.K. offers included £80 off the 13-inch M4 iPad Air with 128GB. Those prices show why it’s worth checking previous selling prices as well as today’s discount: an offer below Apple’s current asking price may still cost more than the same iPad did earlier in the year.
This Black Friday, we’d watch the M4 iPad Air for a balance of performance and price, the A16 iPad for a worthwhile budget deal, and the M5 iPad Pro for buyers who need its premium capabilities. The new A20 Pro iPad mini, with its OLED display, also changes the calculation: we’d expect smaller initial discounts on the new arrival, while remaining A17 Pro stock could offer clearance bargains. Below, we explain which deals are worth taking, checking the generation, storage, and connectivity rather than simply choosing the biggest advertised saving. For offers across Apple’s other products, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.
Which iPad should you buy this Black Friday?


M4 iPad Air – Our best all-round choice

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Air offers a strong balance of performance, screen size, and price without the premium cost of the Pro. The 11-inch model suits buyers who prioritize portability, while the 13-inch version gives you more room for multitasking and creative work.
A good Black Friday discount could make either size an attractive purchase. Compare storage capacities carefully, though: a larger advertised saving on a high-capacity model isn’t necessarily better value if you don’t need the extra space.
U.S. Black Friday price: Amazon is matching Prime Day right now, with $99 off nearly all iPad Air models. Last Black Friday, the previous-generation M3 models were $449 and $649 respectively, which is $150 off and we hope that by Black Friday the deal will be that big. 
U.K. Black Friday price:  There’s £49 off the 128GB 13-inch iPad Air, which is a good saving, although we saw better during Prime Day this October when there was as much as £144 off. Last Black Friday, selected M3 Air configurations received £100 discounts.






iPad Pro – Best for demanding creative work

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Pro is the option for buyers who need Apple’s highest-end tablet performance and premium display. It comes in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes, but its capabilities – and price – will exceed what many people need for browsing, streaming, and everyday apps.
We’d look for a substantial saving rather than buy simply because it’s the most powerful iPad. Compare discounted M4 Pro stock, too: an older Pro could offer better value if its price is sufficiently below the equivalent M5 configuration.
U.S. Black Friday price:  During October Prime Day, the 11-inch M5 Pro with 256GB was $1,099, saving $100. So far we’re seeing nearly $100 off a 1TB 11-inch iPad Pro and up to $150 off the 13-inch iPad Pro. 
U.K. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought little to recommend on the M5 Pro, with reductions of around £12. Last Black Friday, older M4 Pro offers included a saving of approximately £206 at Amazon. Currently the biggest saving is £36 off the entry-level 11-inch model.






iPad (A16) – Our budget choice, at the right price

				
					

				
			
Apple




The A16 iPad remains a capable option for browsing, streaming, schoolwork, and everyday use. However, Apple raised its starting price by $100/£100 in June, and it doesn’t support Apple Intelligence.
That makes the final purchase price particularly important. A modest discount from today’s higher asking price may still leave you paying more than this iPad previously cost. With a replacement expected early in 2027, we’d look for a substantial Black Friday saving and compare the price with discounted iPad Air models before buying.
U.S. Black Friday price: The 128GB A16 iPad was $399 during October Prime Day, saving $50 against its increased $449 price. Last Black Friday, it briefly reached $279. This Black Friday we are already seeing $49 off the 128GB iPad. However, at $399.99, this isn’t an offer we’d rush to buy. It approximately matches October’s $399 price and is well above the $279 we saw last Black Friday. We’d wait for a better discount as Black Friday approaches.
U.K. Black Friday price: October coverage listed the 256GB model at £499.97, around £29 off. Last Black Friday, the 128GB version was £299 and the 256GB version £399 and we hope to see prices go even lower this year, but so far we’re just seeing £30 off the iPad. 






iPad mini with A20 Pro – Best for portability

				
					

				
			
Apple




The new iPad mini went on sale on November 6, replacing the A17 Pro model. It brings an 8.5-inch OLED display, the A20 Pro chip, and a thinner, lighter design, making it the option to consider if you want a compact iPad with the latest hardware.
Because it has only just arrived, we’d expect initial discounts to be smaller than clearance savings on its predecessor. The older A17 Pro mini could still be worthwhile at a sufficiently low price, but compare the saving with what you give up – particularly the new display.
U.S. Black Friday price: The A20 Pro mini wasn’t available during October Prime Day or last Black Friday. Its 128GB A17 Pro predecessor was $499 during October Prime Day and $399 last Black Friday. Unsurprisingly there are no discounts on the new models – you can save around $30 on the price of the A17 Pro iPad mini, but it still costs $70 more than the $499 offer we saw during October Prime Day.
U.K. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought only a small saving on the A17 Pro mini in our coverage. Last Black Friday, its 128GB version reached £449, saving £50. We’re already seeing £100 off the A17 Pro iPad mini this Black Friday month.

Should you buy an iPad now or wait for a better deal?

				
					

				
			
There’s an iPad for everyone.

Foundry




With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an iPad immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so an early offer can be worth taking if the price is competitive. Compare the exact generation, screen size, storage, and connectivity rather than waiting for Black Friday simply because a larger discount might appear.
Previous selling prices are particularly important this year because Apple raised iPad prices in June. During October Prime Day, the 128GB A16 iPad was $399, while the 11-inch M4 iPad Air with 128GB was $649. Both were discounted against Apple’s increased prices, but cost more than their regular prices before June. A saving from today’s asking price doesn’t necessarily mean you’re getting an exceptional bargain.
For the M4 iPad Air and M5 iPad Pro, we’d focus on finding a good price: our guide to the best time to buy an iPad doesn’t expect replacements until 2027. We’d be more cautious about the A16 iPad, which lacks Apple Intelligence and is expected to be replaced. Unless you find a substantial saving, waiting could get you a more capable entry-level model.
The new A20 Pro iPad mini presents a different decision. It has only just arrived, so we’d expect smaller initial discounts rather than immediate clearance-level savings. If you want its OLED display and newer processor, a modest reduction may still be worthwhile. If price matters more, compare remaining A17 Pro stock – but make sure the saving justifies choosing the older hardware.






Should you buy an older iPad? 

				
					

				
			
Foundry




An older iPad can be a good buy if its price reflects its age and the features you give up. Compare its actual selling price with the discounted price of its replacement, matching screen size, storage, and connectivity where possible. A large saving from an old launch price doesn’t necessarily make it better value.
The M3 iPad Air and M4 iPad Pro are worth considering at substantial clearance discounts. Both remain capable options, and you may get more benefit from a lower price or additional storage than from the latest processor. However, if the newer equivalent costs only slightly more, the saving may not justify choosing the older generation.
The A17 Pro iPad mini also deserves consideration now that the A20 Pro model has arrived. It supports Apple Intelligence and remains a capable compact tablet, but you miss the newer model’s OLED display, faster processor, and thinner, lighter design. We’d want a meaningful saving rather than a small reduction from its former asking price.
Be more cautious with much older models. Check whether they support the current version of iPadOS and the apps and features you need. Compatibility today doesn’t guarantee how many future software upgrades they’ll receive. Apple Intelligence support also varies: don’t assume every older Air, Pro, or mini includes it.
If you already own an Apple Pencil or keyboard, check compatibility before changing generations. Keeping compatible accessories could make an older iPad better value, while replacing them could erase part of your saving. Our iPad buying guide explains the differences between the ranges.






iPad deals to avoid
Check the exact configuration before comparing offers. Retailer listings can emphasize iPad, Air, or Pro without making the generation obvious. Confirm the chip, screen size, storage capacity, and whether you’re buying Wi-Fi or Wi-Fi + Cellular. A cheaper listing may be a different model rather than a better deal.
Don’t let a large advertised discount tempt you into paying for storage or connectivity you won’t use. A heavily reduced high-capacity or cellular iPad can still cost more than a simpler configuration that meets your needs. Compare the final purchase prices, rather than assuming the biggest saving represents the best value.
Check whether the price includes nano-texture glass, too. This optional finish reduces glare and makes fingerprints and oily smudges less noticeable, which can be useful if reflections make your iPad difficult to see in bright rooms or outdoors. It avoids much of the washed-out appearance associated with ordinary matte finishes, but contrast can drop at some viewing angles and the surface may be more scratch-sensitive. Availability depends on the model and storage configuration, so you could end up paying for both the finish and additional storage. If reflections rarely bother you, standard glass may be better value. Read our guide to nano-texture glass and whether you need it.
Our iPad buying guide considers cellular a luxury for most buyers. If you mainly use your iPad somewhere with Wi-Fi, you may get little benefit from the extra hardware. For occasional use elsewhere, sharing your iPhone’s connection through Personal Hotspot can be a more economical option.
Cellular makes more sense if you regularly need an independent connection while commuting or traveling; it also adds built-in GPS for accurate location tracking. Factor in any data-plan charges and compare the total cost of a contract with buying outright. A cellular model can still be worthwhile if its sale price matches or beats the equivalent Wi-Fi version—you don’t have to activate a data plan simply because the hardware is included.
Judge savings against previous selling prices as well as Apple’s current price. Following June’s price increases, a discounted iPad may still cost more than it did earlier in the year. Also distinguish a cash discount from a gift-card offer: a gift card doesn’t reduce the amount you pay for the iPad and is useful only if you’ll spend it.
Check what any bundle includes. A keyboard, case, or stylus doesn’t automatically make an offer better value, particularly if the accessories aren’t the versions you want. Read the conditions attached to “free” iPads, trade-in promotions, contracts, and rebates before comparing their total cost with buying outright.
Finally, check whether the iPad is new, refurbished, or used, who is selling it, and what warranty and returns policy apply. For used or refurbished models, look for information about battery condition and confirm that Activation Lock has been removed. Be cautious about devices that remain tied to a previous owner or an organization’s management system.






How we choose iPad deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on iPad reviews and everyday use. We consider performance, display quality, portability, battery life, and accessory support alongside price to explain which iPads suit different buyers.
Our reviews help us assess whether paying more brings practical benefits. A faster processor or premium display may matter for demanding creative work, while a less expensive iPad can be perfectly capable of browsing, streaming, and schoolwork. We also consider the cost of keyboards, Apple Pencils, and other accessories when judging an iPad’s value.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous offers, matching the generation, screen size, storage, and connectivity so that comparisons reflect what you’re actually buying. Following Apple’s June price increases, we also consider earlier selling prices rather than relying solely on savings against today’s recommended price.
Older models can be worthwhile clearance purchases, but only when their prices make sense alongside newer alternatives. Our iPad buying guide explains the differences between the ranges, while our purchase-timing guide helps you decide whether to buy now or wait.

title: Apple releases firmware 9B47 for all AirPods with H2 chip
content:
Macworld





If you have any AirPods with an H2 chip, it’s time for an update. Apple has released firmware version 9B47 for all AirPods that use the H2. That includes:
AirPods Pro 2
AirPods Pro 3
AirPods 4
AirPods 5
AirPods Max 2
The previous firmware was 9A348 which added support from Custom EQ and GymKit. A version 9A350 was released just for the AirPods 5, to bring them up to date with those features.
Apple has not yet disclosed the contents of this release on its AirPods Firmware page. It’s likely this is just “bug fixes and performance improvements,” as there aren’t any new iOS or macOS features that should require new firmware.
You can’t update your AirPods firmware manually. But there are steps you can take to check your firmware version and make sure that Apple updates your AirPods sooner rather than later.
How to update AirPods on iPhone, iPad, or Mac
Make sure that your AirPods are in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad, or Mac. Make sure that device is connected to Wi-Fi.
Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid.
Plug in the charging case (plug the USB cable into a power adapter and the charging case).
Keep the lid of the charging case closed.
Wait at least 30 minutes.
Open the lid of the charging case to reconnect your AirPods to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.
Check the firmware version again.
How to check the firmware version of your AirPods
On iPhone or iPad: With your AirPods nearby and the case open, open Settings on your iPhone or iPad. You’ll see your AirPods listed at the top of Settings. Tap that, and scroll down to the bottom of your AirPods settings to see the Version.
On Mac: Open System Settings. Select Bluetooth, then click the (i) next to your connected AirPods. The Version will be listed there, along with other information.

title: iFixit's PROLED MacBook Pro Teardown Reveals Logo LEDs
content:
iFixit today took apart Apple's touchscreen PROLED MacBook Pro to see how Apple shed weight, what powers the logo, and how it compares to the 14-inch M6 ‌MacBook Pro‌.



Apple added a glowing logo on the back of the PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌, but since there's no backlight to illuminate it, Apple used four LEDs, a reflective layer, and a diffuser to create an even glow. When the light is off, the logo's two-way mirror coating gives it a shiny finish.

OLED.

Apple says the PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌ has a hinge designed for touch, but iFixit said it's basically identical to the M6 ‌MacBook Pro‌'s hinge, just stiffer, so it better holds its angle when the display is tapped at the top.

The Thunderbolt/USB-C ports and fans are replaceable, but the logic board has to come out. The HDMI port and SDXC card slot are soldered to the logic board, so they're not as easily replaced. The SSD and memory are also soldered.

Touch ID. iFixit said the touchscreen didn't add any new parts pairing problems.

The PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌'s trackpad is a little bit smaller than the M6 model's, and weight was shed by removing some aluminum from the lower chassis. The lower case weighs 364 grams vs. 456 grams for the M6 model. The display assembly is 101 grams lighter despite the touchscreen and the glowing Apple logo, and the battery is two grams lighter too.

Does Apple have sales?
Apple rarely discounts its own products. Even during its annual Black Friday shopping event, which runs from Black Friday to Cyber Monday, Apple typically offers gift cards with eligible purchases instead of cutting prices.
That doesn’t mean you have to pay full price. Third-party retailers such as Amazon, Best Buy and other Apple resellers regularly discount Apple products throughout the year.
Some of the best savings on Apple products come during Amazon’s Prime Day events. We saw substantial discounts during Prime Day in June 2026, and another Amazon Prime Day sale takes place on October 6 and 7, when we expect to see more deals on Macs, iPads, AirPods and other Apple devices.
Apple also offers year-round education discounts to students, teachers and education staff. During its annual Back To School promotion – usually running for around three months from June or July in many countries (and from January in Australia, New Zealand and other Southern Hemisphere markets) – eligible higher education students can receive a free pair of AirPods or an Apple Pencil with selected Mac and iPad purchases.
Finally, don’t overlook the Apple Certified Refurbished Store, where you can buy refurbished Macs, iPads and other Apple products at a discount. These devices are thoroughly tested, include a new battery and outer casing where applicable, and come with the same one-year warranty as new Apple products. Following Apple’s June 2026 price increases, some refurbished models can be particularly attractive because their prices haven’t risen in the same way as equivalent new models.
 FAQ 


1.
When are the best Apple deals? 
Apple deals are generally best during major retail events like Black Friday and Amazon Prime Day, or specifically for students during Apple’s annual “Back to School” promotion. While Apple itself rarely offers direct price cuts on new hardware, third-party resellers frequently discount products throughout the year.
The optimal time to buy depends heavily on the product’s release cycle and the specific retailer, though: 
iPhones: The best time to buy is often in the spring or summer, several months after the September launch, when third-party resellers begin offering deeper discounts . Conversely, the worst time is August, just before new models arrive and trigger price drops on older generations.
Macs and iPads: These see significant discounts during Black Friday (late November) and Amazon Prime Day (typically July and October). For students, the Back to School event (running June–September in the U.S. and July–October in the U.K.) is ideal, as Apple often bundles free accessories like AirPods or Apple Pencils with purchases.
Apple Watch: Major savings are typically found during Black Friday and Prime Day events.





2.
Are Apple refurbished deals worth it?
Apple refurbished deals are widely considered worth it, particularly when purchasing directly from the official Apple Refurbished Store, where products are restored to a “like-new” condition. While third-party resellers often provide steeper discounts, Apple’s own process is uniquely rigorous, offering a balance of significant savings and the same protections as a brand-new purchase. 
Buying directly from Apple is often described as “almost indistinguishable” from buying new. According to our guide How much can you save at Apple’s Refurbished Store?, the company puts every device through a “stringent refurbishment process” that includes full functional testing, thorough cleaning, and inspection.
Key benefits of the official Apple Refurbished Store include:
Hardware Replacements: Refurbished iPads and iPhones receive a brand-new battery and outer shell .
Warranty and Support: All products come with a standard one-year limited warranty, 90 days of technical support, and are eligible for AppleCare .
Full Accessories: Devices are repackaged in a plain white box with all original manuals and cables .
Savings: You can typically save around 15% off the retail price for recent models, with much higher discounts on older generations.
Avoid the Apple price hikes: Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store sells products at the old, pre-hike prices – meaning you can effectively sidestep the recent price increases entirely. 





3.
Is it better to buy Apple products from Amazon or Apple?
Deciding whether to buy Apple products from Amazon or directly from Apple depends on whether you prioritize immediate cost savings or the specific perks and guarantees offered by the manufacturer. While Amazon often provides deeper discounts, Apple offers unique benefits like trade-in credits, education pricing, and the assurance of receiving the latest models.





4.
Does Apple ever discount products directly?
Apple rarely provides direct price reductions on its new products, preferring to maintain steady Old MSRP pricing throughout a product’s lifecycle. Instead of traditional discounts, the company typically utilizes alternative methods to provide value directly to consumers, such as gift card incentives during major shopping events, education pricing, and a dedicated refurbished store. 
While you will not often see a lower price tag on a new iPhone or Mac at the Apple Store, the company does offer several ways to save:
Apple Shopping Events: During events like Black Friday and Cyber Monday, Apple typically offers gift cards rather than price cuts. For example, in the 2025 holiday season, Apple provided gift cards ranging from $25 to $250 for eligible purchases.
Education Store: Students, teachers, and higher education staff can access year-round discounts on Macs and iPads . During the annual “Back to School” event, Apple often includes a “freebie” like AirPods or an Apple Pencil with qualifying purchases.
Apple Refurbished Store: This is the primary way to get a direct price reduction from Apple. Products are fully reconditioned, come with a one-year warranty, and can be discounted by hundreds of dollars or pounds.
Trade-In Program: Apple allows customers to trade in old devices to receive credit toward a new purchase, effectively lowering the out-of-pocket cost.

title: Best Apple Watch Black Friday deals: Savings on Series 12, 11, SE, and Ultra
content:
Macworld






Best Black Friday Apple Watch deals so far: U.S.
Apple Watch Ultra 4: $699.99 ($99 off, MSRP $799) – already the best price we’ve seen




Best Black Friday Apple Watch deals so far: U.K.
Apple Watch Ultra 4: £729 (£20 off, RRP £749) – the best price we’ve seen so far
Apple Watch Ultra 3: £519 (£230 less than Apple Watch Ultra 4) – the best price we’ve seen




PRICES CHECKED 10 NOVEMBER, 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November
Black Friday is a great time to buy an Apple Watch, with retailers discounting everything from the affordable SE to the premium Ultra. Last year’s U.S. offers included $50 off the SE 3, up to $70 off the then-new Series 11, and $100 off the Ultra 3. Older models brought bigger savings, including $150 off the Series 10 and $200 off the Ultra 2. In the U.K., clearance offers were particularly attractive: the Series 10 was up to £130 off at Currys, while Argos cut £200 from the Ultra 2’s original price.
October Prime Day brought discounts on this year’s models, too. In the U.S., the 42mm Series 12 fell to $349, the 40mm SE 3 to $199, and the Ultra 4 to $774 – savings of $50, $50, and $25 respectively. U.K. highlights included the SE 3 at £199 and the previous-generation Series 11 at £259.
This Black Friday, we’d watch the Series 12 for discounts on our best Apple Watch for most people, the SE 3 for an affordable entry point, and the Ultra 4 for longer battery life and outdoor features. Remaining Series 11 and Ultra 3 stock could offer particularly good value if priced sufficiently below their replacements. Below, we explain which offers are worth taking and when to wait; for savings across Apple’s other products, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.
Which Apple Watch should you buy this Black Friday?


Apple Watch Series 12 – Our best overall choice

				
					

				
			

Apple




The Series 12 is the Apple Watch we recommend for most people. It combines Apple’s new Health Sensing System, more frequent heart-rate measurements, a Readiness score, and a tougher display with up to 24 hours of battery life.
A worthwhile Black Friday discount could make it an attractive purchase, but compare it with remaining Series 11 stock. The older model has the same quoted battery life, so a substantial saving may outweigh the newer health features.
U.S. Black Friday price: During October Prime Day, the 42mm GPS Series 12 fell to $349, while the 46mm version reached $399 – $50 off each. Last Black Friday, its predecessor, the Series 11, received discounts of up to $70. So far this Black Friday month we’ve seen prices drop by $9, but we expect they will drop further.
U.K. Black Friday price: We didn’t see Series 12 discounts during October Prime Day and so far this November there have been no price drops, but we are hopeful.  


						

							


Apple Watch Ultra 4 – Best for battery life and outdoor adventures

				
					

				
			

Apple




The Ultra 4 is our choice for endurance athletes, outdoor enthusiasts, and buyers who prioritize battery life. It offers up to 50 hours of normal use, satellite communication, precision dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and Apple’s new Health Sensing System.
It’s more watch than most people need, but the current $699.99 offer is substantially below October Prime Day’s $774 price, making it worth considering if you want the latest Ultra. Compare it with the Ultra 3, though, which retains many of its outdoor features but has a shorter 42-hour battery-life rating.
U.S. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought the Ultra 4 down to $774, a $25 saving. This November we’ve already seen the Apple Watch Ultra 4 for $699.99 on Amazon: that’s $99 off. 
U.K. Black Friday price: The Ultra 4 remained at its full £749 price during October Prime Day, but we’ve already seen it drop by £20 to £729 at Amazon. 


						

							


Apple Watch SE 3 – Our best budget choice

				
					

				
			
Apple / Amazon




The SE 3 is the best-value option for buyers who want the core Apple Watch experience. It includes an always-on display, temperature sensing, fast charging, and the S10 chip, but lacks ECG, blood oxygen monitoring, and the newer Health Sensing System.
It remains part of Apple’s current lineup despite launching in 2025. A strong Black Friday offer could make it an excellent affordable purchase, although its previous discounts mean there’s little reason to settle for a token reduction.
U.S. Black Friday price: Both last Black Friday and October Prime Day brought the 40mm GPS model to $199 and the 44mm version to $229 – $50 below their regular prices. So far, the U.S. price drop is just $9 at Amazon, so we’d hold out for bigger savings.
U.K. Black Friday price: Black Friday 2025 and October Prime Day brought the 40mm GPS model to £199 and the 44mm version to £229, saving £20. So far we haven’t seen any price drops for Black Friday 2026.


						

							


Apple Watch Ultra 3 – Best clearance option for outdoor enthusiasts

				
					

				
			
Apple




The Ultra 3 is worth considering if you want a rugged Apple Watch without paying for the latest model. It offers satellite communication, dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and up to 42 hours of battery life.
You give up the Ultra 4’s longer battery life and newer Health Sensing System. Compare their actual selling prices: the Ultra 3 needs to be sufficiently cheaper to justify choosing the older generation.
U.S. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the Ultra 3 fell to $699, a $100 saving. Our October Prime Day coverage found only used models, so it didn’t identify a comparable new-stock offer. So far this November we’ve seen the Apple Watch Ultra 3 for $649, but that’s only $51 cheaper than the Ultra 4, so we’d favor the newer model.  
U.K. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the Ultra 3 was £719, or £30 off. October Prime Day listed it at £569. The price is even lower this November – you can get it for £519 at Amazon, £230 less than the usual Apple Watch Ultra 4 price. 


						

							


Apple Watch Series 11 – Best clearance option for everyday use

				
					

				
			
Apple Watch Series 11




The Series 11 could be a better-value everyday watch than the Series 12 if the price gap is large enough. It has the same quoted 24-hour battery life, although it misses the newer Health Sensing System and Audio Intelligence features.
For buyers who don’t need those additions, a substantial clearance discount could be more useful than a small saving on the latest model.
U.S. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the 42mm GPS Series 11 reached $339, while the 46mm version was $359 – savings of $60 and $70, respectively. Our October Prime Day coverage found only used models in the U.S. and so far that’s all we are seeing this November.
U.K. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought the 42mm Series 11 to £259 and the 46mm version to £299. Last Black Friday’s bigger clearance offers were on the preceding Series 10, which was available for £279 in 42mm and £299 in 46mm. In November 2026 you can get a Series 11 for £299, £120 less than the equivalent Series 12.


						

							







Should you buy an Apple Watch now or wait for a better deal?
With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an Apple Watch immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer matches or comes close to a previous low for the same model and configuration, it can be worth taking – particularly if you want a specific size, color, or band combination.
October Prime Day prices provide useful benchmarks. In the U.S., the Series 12 fell to $349 for the 42mm GPS model and $399 for the 46mm version, while the Ultra 4 reached $774. The SE 3 was $199 in 40mm and $229 in 44mm. Those SE prices also appeared last Black Friday, so we’d look for offers matching or beating them. In the U.K., October highlights included the 40mm SE 3 at £199 and the older 42mm Series 11 at £259.
The Series 12 and Ultra 4 only arrived in September, so finding a better price is the main reason to wait. If you don’t need a watch immediately, those previous offers give you a useful starting point for deciding whether to buy now or hold out.
Compare retailers, too. Last Black Friday, Walmart offered $150 off the Series 10, while U.K. shoppers could find up to £130 off at Currys and £200 off the Ultra 2’s original price at Argos. Our guide to the best time to buy an Apple Watch has more advice on choosing when to purchase.


						

							


Should you buy an older Apple Watch?

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t assume an older Apple Watch is a bad buy. The Series 11 and Ultra 3 are only one generation old and can make excellent purchases if they’re substantially cheaper than the Series 12 or Ultra 4. Both retain many of their replacements’ core features, although you miss the newer Health Sensing System and, with the Ultra 3, the Ultra 4’s longer battery life.
Compare actual selling prices, matching case size, material, connectivity, and band where possible. A $50 difference between a Series 11 and Series 12 may not be enough to justify giving up the newer model’s health features, whereas a substantially larger saving could change the calculation. A discounted Series 11 could also be worth considering alongside the SE 3 if a small premium gets you features you’ll use.
Be much more cautious with the Series 8, SE 2, and original Ultra: those models cannot run watchOS 27. The Series 9 is the oldest standard Apple Watch compatible with the latest software, while the Ultra 2 is the oldest supported Ultra and the SE 3 is the only supported SE. Missing the latest software doesn’t make an older watch unusable, but it makes it harder to recommend as a purchase today.
The Series 9, Series 10, and Ultra 2 can still be worth considering at sufficiently low prices. However, compatibility with today’s software doesn’t guarantee how many future upgrades they’ll receive. Weigh the savings against the watch’s age and features, rather than assuming every supported generation offers equally good value.


						

							


Apple Watch deals to avoid 

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t let a bigger advertised discount tempt you into paying more for a cellular Apple Watch you won’t use. If your iPhone is usually nearby, a GPS model can already handle calls, messages, and notifications through your phone. It can also track runs, use Apple Pay, and play downloaded music without your iPhone. As our experience testing a cellular Apple Watch showed, the extra connectivity may add little to everyday use.
Cellular is worth considering if you regularly leave your iPhone behind and want to remain contactable without Wi-Fi, or you’re setting up a watch for a child without an iPhone. Otherwise, you could pay extra for the hardware and then add an ongoing mobile-plan charge for a feature you rarely need. You don’t have to activate a plan on a cellular model, so it can still be a good buy if its sale price matches or beats the GPS version. Our GPS versus cellular Apple Watch guide explains the trade-offs.
Check the rest of the configuration, too. A premium case material or expensive band can make a heavily discounted watch cost more than a simpler version that meets your needs. Judge offers against previous selling prices as well as the advertised reduction: a large saving from the original launch price doesn’t necessarily mean exceptional value. Check any spending requirements, contracts, trade-ins, or rebates attached to offers advertising a “free” Apple Watch.
Finally, check whether you’re buying a new, refurbished, or used watch, who is selling it, and what warranty and returns policy apply. For a used or refurbished model, check the stated battery condition and confirm that it has been removed from the previous owner’s account and Activation Lock. Make sure the watch is compatible with your iPhone before ordering.


						

							


How we choose Apple Watch deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on Apple Watch reviews and everyday wear. We consider comfort, performance, battery life, charging, health and fitness features, and value – not just the specifications or advertised saving.
Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our Series 12 review assessed battery life and charging performance alongside its newer health features. We also draw on everyday experience: our cellular Apple Watch testing examines whether staying connected without an iPhone justified the extra hardware and subscription costs.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. We check the generation, case size, material, connectivity, and included band so that comparisons reflect what you’re actually buying. Older models can be worthwhile clearance purchases, but only when their prices make sense alongside discounted replacements.
Our Best Apple Watch guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the right choice: your budget, wrist size, activities, and the features you need all matter.
For more offers, visit our Black Friday coverage and our roundups of the best Mac deals, iPad deals, and AirPods deals.

title: iPad Mini 2021 vs. 2026 Buyer's Guide: Is It Worth Upgrading?
content:
Apple's eighth-generation iPad mini went on sale earlier this month with a larger OLED display, a thinner and lighter design, the A20 Pro chip, and water and dust resistance. If you still use the sixth-generation ‌iPad mini‌ from 2021, the upgrade also brings changes that debuted on the 2024 model, including Apple Intelligence, Apple Pencil Pro support, and twice the USB-C transfer speed.


The new ‌iPad mini‌ starts at $699 for 128GB with Wi-Fi or $849 with cellular in the United States. The discontinued 2021 model started at $499 and $649, respectively, with 64GB of storage. Both support iPadOS 27.2, have Touch ID in the top button, and are rated for up to 10 hours of web browsing over Wi-Fi or watching video. Both displays also run at 60Hz.
